lessons.title: Spark architecture: driver, executors, cluster manager
lessons.summary: A Spark application is one driver process plus many executor processes.
lessons.remember: The driver plans, the executors do the work one partition per task, and the cluster manager supplies the machines.

lessons.title: SparkSession, SparkContext and running locally
lessons.summary: SparkSession is the single entry point to Spark in modern code.
lessons.remember: SparkSession is the one door into Spark; SparkContext is the older, lower-level door it wraps.

lessons.title: RDD vs DataFrame (and a note on Dataset)
lessons.summary: Spark has three data abstractions: - RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset): a distributed collection of arbitrary objects.
lessons.remember: In PySpark, use DataFrames; RDDs are a low-level escape hatch and Dataset is a Scala and Java idea.

lessons.title: Lazy evaluation: transformations and actions
lessons.summary: Spark operations come in two kinds: - Transformations (select, filter, join, groupBy, withColumn) return a new DataFrame and only add a step to a plan.
lessons.remember: Transformations build a plan; only actions run it, and every action runs it again unless you cache.

lessons.title: The DAG and RDD lineage
lessons.summary: When an action runs, Spark turns the optimised plan into a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of steps.
lessons.remember: Spark splits the DAG into stages at shuffles, and uses lineage to recompute lost partitions instead of keeping copies.

lessons.title: Schemas and data types
lessons.summary: Every DataFrame has a schema: an ordered list of column names, types and nullability, held as a StructType of StructFields.
lessons.remember: Declare schemas for text sources and use decimals for money; inference is a convenience, not a contract.

lessons.title: Columns, expressions, select and filter
lessons.summary: DataFrame code is built from column expressions.
lessons.remember: A column is an expression, not data; build logic from expressions so Spark can optimise it.

lessons.title: Working with nulls
lessons.summary: Spark SQL follows SQL's null rules: any comparison with null gives null, and a filter keeps only rows where the condition is true.
lessons.remember: Null is "unknown", so comparisons with it are never true; test for it explicitly and use null-safe equality where two unknowns should match.

lessons.title: Sorting, distinct, limit and sampling
lessons.summary: Four everyday operations with very different costs: - orderBy / sort produces a total order across all partitions.
lessons.remember: Global sorts and distincts shuffle everything; ask whether you need them before you write them.

lessons.title: groupBy, aggregation, rollup and cube
lessons.summary: groupBy(keys).agg(...) collapses rows with the same key into one row and computes aggregate expressions: sum, count, avg, min, max, countDistinct, collectlist, first, percentileapprox and many more.
lessons.remember: groupBy shuffles once and aggregates partially first; rollup and cube add subtotal rows marked by grouping().

lessons.title: Joins in Spark
lessons.summary: df.join(other, on, how) combines two DataFrames.
lessons.remember: Join on column names to avoid duplicate keys, use leftsemi and leftanti for existence checks, and watch for key duplication.

lessons.title: Union and set operations
lessons.summary: - union(other) appends rows by position.
lessons.remember: Use unionByName, not union, unless you have checked column order yourself.

lessons.title: Pivot and unpivot
lessons.summary: Pivot turns distinct values of one column into new columns, with an aggregate in each cell: groupBy("product").pivot("month").sum("qty").
lessons.remember: Pivot with an explicit values list; unpivot wide legacy tables into rows early.

lessons.title: Explode and nested data
lessons.summary: JSON, Avro and API data often contain arrays and nested structs.
lessons.remember: explode turns array elements into rows; use explodeouter to keep empty ones and never explode two arrays blindly.

lessons.title: Window functions in Spark
lessons.summary: A window function computes a value for each row from a window of related rows, without collapsing them like groupBy does.
lessons.remember: Windows compute per-row results over related rows; always state the frame when you mean rows, and partition by a key.

lessons.title: Deduplication patterns
lessons.summary: Two kinds of duplicates need two tools: - Exact or key duplicates where any copy will do: dropDuplicates("key") keeps one arbitrary row per key.
lessons.remember: dropDuplicates keeps any copy; when one copy must win, rank with rownumber and a full tie-breaking order.

lessons.title: Built-in functions: string, date, math, conditional
lessons.summary: pyspark.sql.functions (imported as F) holds hundreds of functions that run inside the JVM: - String: upper, trim, concatws, substring, split, regexpreplace, lpad, formatstring.
lessons.remember: Reach for pyspark.sql.functions first; a built-in is almost always faster than anything you write in Python.

lessons.title: Arrays, maps, structs, JSON and regex
lessons.summary: Spark handles nested data natively: - Structs group fields: F.struct(...) builds one, col("a.b") reads one.
lessons.remember: Parse JSON once with a schema, and use higher-order functions to work inside arrays without exploding them.

lessons.title: Python UDFs
lessons.summary: A user-defined function (UDF) runs your own Python function on each row.
lessons.remember: A Python UDF is a black box that ships every row to Python; use it only when no built-in or pandas UDF fits.

lessons.title: pandas UDFs and Apache Arrow
lessons.summary: A pandas UDF (vectorised UDF) receives whole batches of rows as pandas Series or DataFrames instead of one row at a time.
lessons.remember: pandas UDFs move data in Arrow batches, so Python libraries can run on Spark at near-vectorised speed.

lessons.title: Broadcast variables and accumulators
lessons.summary: Two shared-variable tools from the RDD era that still matter: - A broadcast variable sends a read-only value (a lookup dictionary, a small model) to every executor once, instead of with every task.
lessons.remember: Broadcast ships read-only data once per executor; accumulators in transformations can over-count on retries, so do not use them for exact business numbers.

lessons.title: Spark SQL, views, subqueries and CTEs
lessons.summary: Spark SQL and the DataFrame API are two front ends to the same engine.
lessons.remember: SQL and DataFrames compile to the same plan, so pick whichever reads better for each step.

lessons.title: Catalog, databases and tables
lessons.summary: Spark keeps table definitions in a catalog (metastore).
lessons.remember: Managed tables let the catalog own the files; external tables only point at them, and modern catalogs add a third naming level.

lessons.title: Query hints
lessons.summary: Hints tell the optimiser to choose a plan it might not choose itself.
lessons.remember: Hints override the optimiser; use them for proven problems and revisit them when data volumes change.

lessons.title: Reading and writing data, save modes
lessons.summary: spark.read returns a DataFrameReader: you set format, options and an optional schema, then load a path or table.
lessons.remember: Readers set format, options and schema; writers set format and mode, and only a table format makes overwrite safe.

lessons.title: File formats: CSV, JSON, Parquet, ORC, Avro, and compression
lessons.summary: - CSV: text, row-based, no types, many dialects.
lessons.remember: Land raw data in whatever the source gives you, but store analytical data in a columnar format, usually Parquet under a table format.

lessons.title: XML and Excel files
lessons.summary: Legacy systems often hand over XML or spreadsheets.
lessons.remember: XML is readable natively in Spark 4 (via spark-xml before), while Excel is a small-data, driver-side job.

lessons.title: JDBC reads and writes
lessons.summary: Spark reads from and writes to relational databases through JDBC.
lessons.remember: A JDBC read is single-threaded until you give it a partition column or predicates, and every partition is another connection to the source.

lessons.title: Partitioning and bucketing on disk
lessons.summary: Partitioning on disk (df.write.partitionBy("country", "loaddate")) writes one folder per value: .../country=DE/loaddate=2025-10-15/.
lessons.remember: Partition on disk by a low-cardinality filter column such as date; too many partitions is worse than none.

lessons.title: Partitions, repartition and coalesce
lessons.summary: A DataFrame is split into partitions: chunks of rows processed independently, one task per partition.
lessons.remember: Partitions set parallelism; repartition shuffles to rebalance, coalesce merges cheaply but only downward.

lessons.title: Shuffle
lessons.summary: A shuffle redistributes rows across partitions so that rows with the same key end up together.
lessons.remember: A shuffle moves rows by key across the network between stages; filter and project before it, and avoid the ones you do not need.

lessons.title: Data skew
lessons.summary: Skew means some keys have far more rows than others.
lessons.remember: Skew is one key with too many rows; check nulls and hot keys, let AQE split joins, broadcast if possible, and salt as a last resort.

lessons.title: Caching and persistence
lessons.summary: Because every action re-runs the plan from the source, a DataFrame used several times is computed several times.
lessons.remember: Cache only what you reuse, materialise it with an action, and unpersist when done.

lessons.title: Broadcast joins and join strategies
lessons.summary: Spark picks a physical join strategy for each join: - Broadcast hash join: the small side is collected and sent to every executor; each task joins its partition of the large side locally.
lessons.remember: Broadcast the small side to avoid shuffling the big one; sort-merge is the safe default for two large tables.

lessons.title: Adaptive Query Execution
lessons.summary: Adaptive Query Execution (AQE), on by default since Spark 3.2, re-optimises a query while it runs, using real statistics collected at each shuffle boundary rather than estimates made before the start.
lessons.remember: AQE re-plans at each shuffle using real sizes: it merges small partitions, switches to broadcast joins, and splits skewed join partitions.

lessons.title: Catalyst optimiser and Tungsten engine
lessons.summary: Every DataFrame or SQL query passes through Catalyst, Spark's optimiser, in four phases: 1.
lessons.remember: Catalyst rewrites and plans the query, Tungsten executes it with compact memory and generated code.

lessons.title: Reading explain plans
lessons.summary: df.explain(mode) prints the plan Spark will run.
lessons.remember: Read plans bottom-up and look at scans for pushed filters, Exchanges for shuffles, and join operators for the strategy.

lessons.title: Partition pruning, column pruning and predicate pushdown
lessons.summary: The fastest data to process is data you never read.
lessons.remember: Filter on stored columns, select only what you need, and lay data out so statistics can skip files.

lessons.title: Memory, spill and garbage collection
lessons.summary: Each executor's JVM heap is divided by Spark's unified memory manager into: - Execution memory: buffers for shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations.
lessons.remember: Spill means partitions are too big for execution memory; out-of-memory means something could not spill, often skew, collect, broadcast or Python.

lessons.title: Jobs, stages, tasks and the Spark UI
lessons.summary: The vocabulary of Spark execution: - Job: what one action triggers.
lessons.remember: An action is a job, shuffles split it into stages, each stage runs one task per partition, and the Spark UI shows where time went.

lessons.title: Delta Lake: ACID tables on files
lessons.summary: Plain Parquet folders have no transactions: a failed write leaves half-written files, readers can see partial results, and you cannot update a row.
lessons.remember: Delta adds a transaction log to Parquet files, giving ACID writes, schema enforcement, MERGE and time travel on a data lake.

lessons.title: MERGE and upserts in Delta
lessons.summary: MERGE INTO combines insert, update and delete in one atomic operation, driven by a join between a source (new or changed rows) and the target table: - WHEN MATCHED AND condition THEN UPDATE SET ...
lessons.remember: MERGE applies inserts, updates and deletes atomically from a deduplicated source; limit the target files it touches.

lessons.title: Time travel, restore and vacuum
lessons.summary: Because Delta never overwrites files in place, older versions of a table remain readable: - Time travel: SELECT FROM t VERSION AS OF 12 or TIMESTAMP AS OF '2025-10-01', or the versionAsOf reader option.
lessons.remember: Delta keeps old versions until VACUUM removes files beyond the retention window; use time travel as undo, not as backup.

lessons.title: Compaction, Z-order and liquid clustering
lessons.summary: Two layout problems slow down Delta tables: 1.
lessons.remember: Compact small files with OPTIMIZE, and cluster on the columns you filter by, preferring liquid clustering for new tables.

lessons.title: Schema enforcement and evolution
lessons.summary: Schema enforcement: Delta rejects writes whose columns or types do not match the table, instead of silently corrupting it.
lessons.remember: Delta enforces the schema by default; allow evolution deliberately, mostly in raw layers.

lessons.title: Change data feed
lessons.summary: The change data feed (CDF) records row-level changes made to a Delta table.
lessons.remember: Change data feed exposes each row's insert, update and delete since a version, so downstream jobs process only changes, including deletes.

lessons.title: Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi
lessons.summary: Delta is one of three widely used open table formats.
lessons.remember: Iceberg is the most engine-neutral format with catalog-based metadata, Hudi targets upsert-heavy pipelines, and Delta dominates Spark-centred platforms.

lessons.title: Slowly changing dimensions in Spark
lessons.summary: A slowly changing dimension (SCD) is a dimension table (customer, product) whose attributes change over time.
lessons.remember: SCD type 1 overwrites, type 2 closes the old row and inserts a new one, and in Delta both are MERGE statements.

lessons.title: Medallion architecture
lessons.summary: The medallion architecture organises lakehouse data into layers of increasing quality: - Bronze (raw): data as received, append-only, with ingestion metadata (source file, load time).
lessons.remember: Bronze keeps raw history, silver cleans and conforms, gold serves the business; the value is in clear responsibilities, not the names.

lessons.title: The Structured Streaming model
lessons.summary: Structured Streaming treats a stream as an unbounded table that keeps growing.
lessons.remember: Structured Streaming runs ordinary DataFrame logic incrementally over an ever-growing table, one micro-batch at a time.

lessons.title: Triggers and output modes
lessons.summary: Triggers decide when micro-batches run: - Default (no trigger): start the next batch as soon as the previous one finishes.
lessons.remember: Triggers set when batches run (availableNow for incremental batch jobs), and output modes set what each batch writes.

lessons.title: Event time, watermarks and windows
lessons.summary: Event time is when something happened (a timestamp in the event); processing time is when Spark sees it.
lessons.remember: Aggregate on event time, and set a watermark so Spark can finalise windows and forget old state.

lessons.title: Stateful operations and state stores
lessons.summary: Some streaming operations must remember data across micro-batches.
lessons.remember: Stateful streaming remembers data per key across batches; always bound it with watermarks or TTLs, and use RocksDB for large state.

lessons.title: Checkpointing and recovery
lessons.summary: Every streaming query writes to a checkpoint location, a folder that records: - Offsets: which source data each micro-batch planned to read (written before processing).
lessons.remember: The checkpoint is the stream's memory of offsets, commits and state; one per query, on durable storage, and change queries with care.

lessons.title: Stream-static and stream-stream joins
lessons.summary: Two kinds of joins on streams: - Stream-static: each micro-batch of the stream is joined with a static DataFrame or table (for example enriching orders with a product dimension).
lessons.remember: Stream-static joins enrich each batch statelessly; stream-stream joins buffer state and need watermarks and time bounds.

lessons.title: Sinks and foreachBatch
lessons.summary: Built-in sinks: Delta and file formats (exactly-once with checkpoints), Kafka (at-least-once), console and memory (testing), and foreach (per row).
lessons.remember: foreachBatch hands each micro-batch to batch code, mostly for MERGE; make it idempotent because batches can be retried.

lessons.title: Kafka, Event Hubs and Kinesis sources
lessons.summary: Spark reads message brokers as streams of records with key, value (binary), topic, partition, offset and timestamp columns.
lessons.remember: Spark reads brokers as offset-tracked binary records, keeps offsets in its checkpoint, and parallelises by topic partition.

lessons.title: Exactly-once and backpressure
lessons.summary: Exactly-once in Structured Streaming means each input record affects the final sink output exactly once, even across failures.
lessons.remember: Exactly-once needs a replayable source, a checkpoint and an idempotent sink; rate limits per batch are Spark's backpressure.

lessons.title: Auto Loader and incremental file ingestion
lessons.summary: Many sources deliver files into cloud storage: daily extracts, exports, logs.
lessons.remember: Load landing-zone files incrementally with a checkpointed file stream; on Databricks, Auto Loader adds scalable discovery and schema evolution.

lessons.title: Cluster managers: YARN, Kubernetes, standalone
lessons.summary: Spark does not manage machines itself.
lessons.remember: YARN, Kubernetes or standalone supply the machines; the Spark model on top is the same, and managed platforms hide this layer.

lessons.title: spark-submit and deploy modes
lessons.summary: spark-submit launches a Spark application on a cluster.
lessons.remember: spark-submit packages code, dependencies and resources into a job; use cluster mode for production.

lessons.title: Executor sizing and resources
lessons.summary: The main resource settings: - spark.executor.cores: task slots per executor.
lessons.remember: Size executors moderately (around 4 to 5 cores, enough memory and overhead per core) and fix plans before adding memory.

lessons.title: Dynamic allocation and autoscaling
lessons.summary: With dynamic allocation (spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true), Spark requests more executors when tasks are waiting and releases idle ones after a timeout, between minExecutors and maxExecutors.
lessons.remember: Dynamic allocation adds and removes executors with demand; it needs shuffle files to survive executor removal.

lessons.title: Managed Spark platforms compared
lessons.summary: Most organisations run Spark on a managed service rather than their own clusters: - Databricks (AWS, Azure, GCP): Spark plus Photon, Delta Lake, Unity Catalog, notebooks, jobs and serverless compute.
lessons.remember: Spark code moves easily between managed platforms; catalogs, utilities, security and cost models do not.

lessons.title: Validation, profiling and expectations
lessons.summary: Data quality work in Spark has three layers: - Profiling: understanding data before writing rules.
lessons.remember: Profile first, then encode rules that fail, drop or quarantine, and compute them in as few passes as possible.

lessons.title: Reconciliation between source and target
lessons.summary: Reconciliation proves that a target holds the same data as its source, which is essential during migrations and for regulated pipelines.
lessons.remember: Reconcile in layers: counts, aggregates, partition checksums, then row diffs where checksums disagree, after normalising values.

lessons.title: Data lineage (not RDD lineage)
lessons.summary: Data lineage records which datasets, jobs and columns produce which other datasets: "gold.revenue is built by job X from silver.orders and silver.fxrates".
lessons.remember: Data lineage maps datasets and jobs across pipelines; RDD lineage only rebuilds partitions inside one Spark app.

lessons.title: Masking, access control and auditing
lessons.summary: Open-source Spark has little built-in data security: whoever can read the files can read the data.
lessons.remember: Spark's data security lives in the catalog and platform: privileges, row filters, column masks and audit logs, with storage locked to governed compute.

lessons.title: Testing PySpark code with pytest
lessons.summary: PySpark transformations are ordinary Python functions that take and return DataFrames, so they can be unit tested with pytest: - A session-scoped fixture creates one local SparkSession for all tests (starting Spark is sl
lessons.remember: Write transformations as functions of DataFrames and test them with pytest and a shared local session.

lessons.title: Project structure, packaging, configuration and style
lessons.summary: Production Spark code looks like a normal Python project: - Layout: a package (src/pipeline/) with modules for reading, transforming and writing; thin entry-point scripts or notebooks that call it; tests/ beside it.
lessons.remember: Put logic in a tested, versioned package, keep notebooks and scripts thin, and drive environments from configuration.

lessons.title: Logging, monitoring and debugging
lessons.summary: Three sources of evidence when a Spark job misbehaves: - Logs: the driver log contains your own Python logging and the main error; executor logs contain task-level errors (and Python worker tracebacks for UDFs).
lessons.remember: Use the driver log for your messages, the first JVM "Caused by" for the real error, and the Spark UI for where time went.

lessons.title: CI/CD for Spark jobs
lessons.summary: Continuous integration (CI) runs automatically on every pull request: formatting and lint checks, unit tests with a local Spark session, and building the wheel.
lessons.remember: CI tests and builds on every change; CD deploys the same artefact through environments with configuration and approvals.

lessons.title: Orchestrating Spark with Airflow
lessons.summary: An orchestrator runs jobs in the right order, on schedule, with retries and alerts.
lessons.remember: Airflow schedules and sequences Spark jobs through operators; the processing still happens on the Spark platform.

lessons.title: Idempotency, retries and error handling
lessons.summary: A job is idempotent when running it twice for the same input gives the same result as running it once.
lessons.remember: Design every job so a rerun replaces or merges its own output; then retries and backfills are safe.

lessons.title: Ingestion and extraction patterns
lessons.summary: Getting data out of source systems follows a few patterns: - Full extract: copy the whole table every run.
lessons.remember: Pick full, incremental, CDC, API or file ingestion per source, land data raw with metadata, and interpret it downstream.

lessons.title: Reading Oracle and SQL Server via JDBC
lessons.summary: Migrations from legacy systems usually start with Spark reading Oracle and SQL Server over JDBC.
lessons.remember: Partition JDBC reads, push filters to the source, raise fetch size, and pin types explicitly when extracting from Oracle and SQL Server.

lessons.title: Mainframe extracts and flat files
lessons.summary: Legacy mainframe and midrange systems typically deliver flat files: - Fixed-width records: each field at a fixed position and length, no delimiter.
lessons.remember: Mainframe files need their copybook: fixed widths, EBCDIC, packed decimals and implied decimals must all be decoded deliberately.

lessons.title: Incremental loads and watermark columns
lessons.summary: An incremental load processes only data that is new or changed since the last successful run.
lessons.remember: Read past the stored high-water mark with an overlap, MERGE by key, and move the mark only after a successful write; handle deletes separately.

lessons.title: Backfill and cutover
lessons.summary: Moving a workload from a legacy system to a new platform has two data phases: - Backfill: load history into the new platform.
lessons.remember: Backfill history with the production code, run old and new in parallel with daily reconciliation, then cut over with a rehearsed plan and a rollback window.

lessons.title: pandas API on Spark
lessons.summary: The pandas API on Spark (import pyspark.pandas as ps) lets you write pandas-style code that runs distributed on Spark.
lessons.remember: The pandas API on Spark (formerly Koalas) scales pandas-style code, but indexes and ordering make it less efficient than native DataFrames.

lessons.title: Spark Connect
lessons.summary: Classically, a PySpark program is the driver: your Python process starts a JVM and talks to it directly.
lessons.remember: Spark Connect turns PySpark into a thin gRPC client of a remote Spark server; DataFrames work, RDD and JVM-dependent APIs do not.

lessons.title: Notable Spark 4 changes
lessons.summary: Apache Spark 4.0 was released in May 2025, followed by 4.1 (December 2025) and 4.2 (July 2026).
lessons.remember: Spark 4 makes ANSI errors the default, adds VARIANT, Python data sources and better Spark Connect, and drops old Java, Scala and Mesos.

lessons.title: What Microsoft Fabric is
lessons.summary: Microsoft Fabric is a SaaS analytics platform.
lessons.remember: Fabric is one SaaS platform where every workload shares a capacity for compute and OneLake for storage.

lessons.title: OneLake
lessons.summary: OneLake is the single logical data lake that comes with every Fabric tenant.
lessons.remember: OneLake is one ADLS-based lake per tenant, organised by workspace and item, holding Delta tables that every Fabric engine reads.

lessons.title: Tenants, capacities and workspaces
lessons.summary: Fabric has a four-level containment hierarchy: 1.
lessons.remember: Tenant holds settings and OneLake, capacities supply regional compute, workspaces hold items, and domains group workspaces for governance.

lessons.title: Licensing and capacity units
lessons.summary: Fabric is paid mainly through capacities.
lessons.remember: You buy capacity units that every workload shares; bursting and smoothing absorb spikes, and sustained overuse leads to staged throttling.

lessons.title: Fabric vs Synapse, ADF and Power BI Premium
lessons.summary: Fabric is Microsoft's successor platform for several earlier services: - Azure Synapse Analytics: Fabric Data Warehouse, Fabric Spark, pipelines and Eventhouse cover the same ground as dedicated SQL pools, Synapse Spark,
lessons.remember: Fabric absorbs Synapse, ADF and Power BI Premium, but the mapping is not one-to-one and moving is a project, not a switch.

lessons.title: Lakehouse
lessons.summary: A Lakehouse is a Fabric item that stores data in OneLake and is designed to be written mainly by Spark (notebooks, Spark job definitions) and by Data Factory.
lessons.remember: A Lakehouse is Spark-first storage with a Files area for anything and a Tables area of Delta tables that every Fabric engine can read.

lessons.title: Warehouse
lessons.summary: A Fabric Warehouse is a relational data warehouse you build and load with T-SQL.
lessons.remember: The Warehouse is the T-SQL-first, read-write store in Fabric, with multi-table transactions and Delta storage underneath.

lessons.title: SQL analytics endpoint
lessons.summary: The SQL analytics endpoint is a read-only T-SQL interface that Fabric creates automatically for each lakehouse, mirrored database and SQL database (exactly one per item).
lessons.remember: The SQL analytics endpoint gives read-only T-SQL over lakehouse tables, with a sync delay and with security that protects only the SQL path.

lessons.title: Shortcuts
lessons.summary: A shortcut is a pointer in OneLake to data stored somewhere else.
lessons.remember: A shortcut is a zero-copy pointer to data elsewhere; external shortcuts read with a shared delegated credential.

lessons.title: Mirroring
lessons.summary: Mirroring continuously replicates data from an operational or analytical source into OneLake as Delta tables, without you building pipelines.
lessons.remember: Mirroring is managed, near real-time replication of a source into read-only Delta tables in OneLake, with free replication compute.

lessons.title: Delta format in Fabric
lessons.summary: Delta Lake is Fabric's common table format.
lessons.remember: Everything in Fabric is Delta in OneLake; V-Order and regular compaction decide how fast it reads.

lessons.title: Data Factory pipelines
lessons.summary: A Fabric pipeline orchestrates work: it runs activities in order, with branching, loops, parameters and error paths.
lessons.remember: Fabric pipelines are ADF's orchestration model inside Fabric, minus datasets and SSIS, plus native Fabric activities.

lessons.title: Dataflows Gen2
lessons.summary: Dataflow Gen2 is low-code data preparation with Power Query, the same engine used in Excel and Power BI.
lessons.remember: Dataflow Gen2 is Power Query in Fabric: great for low-code shaping at moderate volume, costly for heavy lifting.

lessons.title: Copy job
lessons.summary: A Copy job is a Fabric item that moves data from a source to a destination without building a pipeline.
lessons.remember: Copy job is managed bulk and incremental copy with built-in state, the simplest way to land source tables in Fabric.

lessons.title: On-premises and VNet data gateways
lessons.summary: Fabric is a cloud service, so it needs a bridge to reach data behind a firewall: - The on-premises data gateway is Windows software you install on a machine inside your network.
lessons.remember: Use the on-premises gateway for data inside your own network and the VNet gateway for private Azure sources; Spark and Direct Lake do not go through gateways.

lessons.title: Notebooks in Fabric
lessons.summary: Fabric notebooks are the main place to write Spark code (PySpark, Spark SQL, Scala, SparkR) against OneLake.
lessons.remember: Fabric notebooks run Spark or plain Python against OneLake, with a default lakehouse and NotebookUtils for orchestration helpers.

lessons.title: Spark pools, environments and runtimes
lessons.summary: Fabric manages Spark clusters for you.
lessons.remember: Starter pools start fast, custom pools fit special needs, and environments pin the runtime and libraries your code needs.

lessons.title: Spark job definitions
lessons.summary: A Spark job definition is a Fabric item that runs a packaged Spark program, much like spark-submit.
lessons.remember: A Spark job definition is Fabric's spark-submit: a packaged program with arguments, environment and retries.

lessons.title: Spark performance features in Fabric
lessons.summary: Fabric adds several features on top of open-source Spark: - Native execution engine: runs supported Spark SQL operators in vectorised C++ (built on the open-source Velox and Apache Gluten projects) instead of the JVM.
lessons.remember: Fabric speeds Spark up with a native C++ engine and session sharing, but the fundamentals of partitioning and shuffle still decide performance.

lessons.title: Real-Time Intelligence overview
lessons.summary: Real-Time Intelligence is Fabric's workload for data in motion: telemetry, logs, clickstreams, IoT readings, change events.
lessons.remember: Real-Time Intelligence chains Eventstream to move, Eventhouse to store and query, dashboards to watch and Activator to act.

lessons.title: Eventstreams
lessons.summary: An Eventstream is a no-code pipeline for events.
lessons.remember: Eventstream connects, shapes and routes events without code, with at-least-once delivery.

lessons.title: Eventhouse and KQL databases
lessons.summary: An Eventhouse is a container for one or more KQL databases, the same engine as Azure Data Explorer.
lessons.remember: Eventhouse is Fabric's engine for fast queries over append-only event data, with an optional Delta copy in OneLake.

lessons.title: Activator
lessons.summary: Activator (formerly Data Activator; items still appear with the type name Reflex) watches data and acts when a condition is met.
lessons.remember: Activator turns conditions in data into alerts and actions, per tracked object.

lessons.title: Real-time dashboards
lessons.summary: A Real-Time Dashboard is a Fabric item whose tiles each run a KQL query against an Eventhouse, Azure Data Explorer or Azure Monitor.
lessons.remember: Real-time dashboards are KQL tiles for live operational monitoring; Power BI reports are for modelled business reporting.

lessons.title: Experiments and ML models
lessons.summary: Fabric's Data Science workload uses MLflow for machine learning bookkeeping, surfaced as two item types: - An experiment item groups training runs.
lessons.remember: Fabric experiments and models are MLflow under the hood, with PREDICT for batch scoring in Spark.

lessons.title: AutoML and ML tooling in Fabric
lessons.summary: AutoML automatically tries algorithms and hyperparameters and returns the best model by a chosen metric.
lessons.remember: Fabric AutoML (FLAML) finds a strong baseline model quickly, but the problem framing and data quality are still your job.

lessons.title: Copilot and AI features
lessons.summary: Fabric embeds generative AI in three ways: - Copilot inside workloads: generating Power Query steps in dataflows, building pipelines, writing SQL and KQL, creating Power BI report pages and summaries, and helping in note
lessons.remember: Copilot helps authors, data agents answer business questions over governed data, and AI functions enrich columns, all on paid capacity.

lessons.title: Semantic models
lessons.summary: A semantic model (formerly a Power BI dataset) is the business layer between data and reports.
lessons.remember: The semantic model is where business definitions and report security live; feed it a clean star schema.

lessons.title: Direct Lake
lessons.summary: Direct Lake is a semantic model storage mode that loads columns from Delta tables in OneLake directly into the VertiPaq engine when queries need them.
lessons.remember: Direct Lake reads OneLake Delta tables straight into Power BI's engine; keep tables compact and watch for fallback.

lessons.title: Reports, dashboards and apps
lessons.summary: Fabric includes the full Power BI service: - Reports: interactive pages of visuals on a semantic model, built in Power BI Desktop or the browser.
lessons.remember: Reports explore, paginated reports print, and apps distribute; security belongs in the model, not the report.

lessons.title: Governance model in Fabric
lessons.summary: Fabric governance is a delegated model: a small central team sets guardrails, and control is pushed down to the people closest to the data.
lessons.remember: Fabric governance flows from tenant to capacity and domain, to workspace, item and finally data-level security, and each layer has its own admin.

lessons.title: Tenant settings and admin portal
lessons.summary: Tenant settings switch Fabric features on or off for the organisation.
lessons.remember: Tenant settings switch features on or off for chosen groups and can be delegated to domains or capacities, but they do not secure data.

lessons.title: Domains
lessons.summary: A domain groups workspaces by business area: Finance, Sales, Manufacturing.
lessons.remember: Domains group workspaces by business area for discovery and delegated settings, but they are not a security boundary.

lessons.title: Workspace roles
lessons.summary: Every workspace has four roles, assigned to users, security groups, Microsoft 365 groups or service principals: Capability Admin Member Contributor Viewer --------------- Manage workspace, delete it, connect to Git Yes A
lessons.remember: Workspace roles are coarse: Contributor and above can read and change all data in the workspace, so design workspaces around who should see what.

lessons.title: Item permissions and sharing
lessons.summary: To give someone access to one item without a workspace role, you share it.
lessons.remember: Sharing grants Read only; ReadData opens the SQL path, ReadAll opens the Spark and file path, and write access needs a workspace role.

lessons.title: OneLake security
lessons.summary: OneLake security (which grew out of "OneLake data access roles") defines roles inside an item that grant access to specific tables, folders or schemas, optionally with row-level and column-level filters.
lessons.remember: OneLake security puts table, row and column permissions on the data itself, so SQL, Spark and Direct Lake all enforce the same rules.

lessons.title: Row, column and object level security
lessons.summary: Inside the Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint, standard T-SQL security applies: - Object-level security: GRANT, DENY, REVOKE on tables, views, functions and procedures.
lessons.remember: T-SQL grants, RLS and masking protect the SQL path and model RLS protects the model; neither stops Spark reads on its own.

lessons.title: Sensitivity labels and DLP
lessons.summary: Sensitivity labels from Microsoft Purview Information Protection (for example Public, General, Confidential, Highly Confidential) can be applied to Fabric items.
lessons.remember: Sensitivity labels classify and travel downstream, DLP detects sensitive data, and protection policies restrict access by label.

lessons.title: Microsoft Purview and the OneLake catalog
lessons.summary: Two catalogs meet here: - The OneLake catalog is Fabric's built-in catalog, with three tabs.
lessons.remember: The OneLake catalog governs what is in Fabric; Purview governs the whole estate and scans Fabric into it.

lessons.title: Lineage and impact analysis
lessons.summary: Fabric captures item-level lineage automatically: which source feeds which pipeline or dataflow, which lakehouse feeds which semantic model, which model feeds which report.
lessons.remember: Fabric lineage is item-level: the lineage view shows a workspace, impact analysis shows everything downstream across workspaces.

lessons.title: Endorsement
lessons.summary: Endorsement marks items that people can trust.
lessons.remember: Promoted is the owner's claim, certified is a reviewer's approval, and master data marks the authoritative source.

lessons.title: Auditing and monitoring
lessons.summary: Fabric has several monitoring tools, each answering a different question: - Audit log (in Microsoft Purview Audit): who did what?
lessons.remember: Audit logs say who did what, the metrics app says how busy the capacity is, and the monitoring hub says whether jobs ran.

lessons.title: Git integration
lessons.summary: Git integration connects a Fabric workspace to a branch in a Git repository: Azure DevOps, GitHub or GitHub Enterprise (cloud versions only).
lessons.remember: Git integration versions Fabric item definitions per workspace branch; data and secrets stay out of Git.

lessons.title: Deployment pipelines
lessons.summary: A deployment pipeline promotes content between workspaces that represent stages, such as Development, Test and Production.
lessons.remember: Deployment pipelines promote item definitions between stage workspaces, with rules and autobinding to point each stage at its own data.

lessons.title: REST APIs and automation
lessons.summary: Everything you do in the Fabric portal can increasingly be automated: - Fabric REST APIs cover workspaces, items and item definitions, Git operations, deployment pipelines, job scheduling, the catalog and admin tasks (do
lessons.remember: REST APIs, the Fabric CLI, fabric-cicd and Terraform let you create and deploy Fabric content from code with service principals.

lessons.title: Lakehouse vs Warehouse (and Eventhouse)
lessons.summary: Fabric offers several stores that all keep data in OneLake.
lessons.remember: Pick the Lakehouse for Spark teams and all data shapes, the Warehouse for T-SQL teams needing transactions, and the Eventhouse for streaming and time series.

lessons.title: Fabric vs Databricks vs Snowflake
lessons.summary: The three platforms overlap heavily: all offer lakehouse-style storage on open formats, SQL warehousing, Spark or Spark-like processing, ML and AI features, and governance.
lessons.remember: Fabric centres on Microsoft and BI, Databricks on engineering and ML, Snowflake on SQL and sharing, and many estates combine them.

lessons.title: Capacity sizing and cost
lessons.summary: Sizing a Fabric capacity is iterative: 1.
lessons.remember: Estimate, prove with the Metrics app, separate risky workloads, reserve the base, and remember viewer licences below F64.

lessons.title: Migrating from legacy platforms to Fabric
lessons.summary: Typical sources and the Fabric tooling for each: - SQL Server, Synapse dedicated SQL pools (and Teradata metadata, preview) to Warehouse: the Migration Assistant for Fabric Data Warehouse imports a DACPAC, SQL scripts or
lessons.remember: Fabric's assistants translate code and schema, but a migration still needs a target design, parallel running and reconciliation.

lessons.title: When not to use Fabric
lessons.summary: Fabric is not the best answer everywhere.
lessons.remember: Avoid or limit Fabric where strict network isolation, multi-cloud, infrastructure control, tiny scale or low-latency serving dominate.

lessons.title: Control plane and compute plane
lessons.summary: Databricks splits its architecture in two: - The control plane runs in Databricks' own cloud account: the web application, notebooks service, job scheduler, cluster manager, Unity Catalog services and APIs.
lessons.remember: The control plane is Databricks' service; compute runs either in your account (classic) or in Databricks' account (serverless), while data stays in object storage.

lessons.title: Accounts and workspaces
lessons.summary: A Databricks account is the top level: it holds identities (users, groups, service principals), single sign-on, billing, Unity Catalog metastores (one per region) and workspaces.
lessons.remember: The account owns identity, billing and metastores; workspaces are where work happens, and many workspaces can share one governed metastore.

lessons.title: Compute types
lessons.summary: Databricks offers several kinds of compute (names as of October 2026): - Serverless compute for notebooks, jobs (Lakeflow Jobs) and pipelines: no cluster configuration, fast start, automatic scaling and upgrades, Photon
lessons.remember: Use serverless where its limits are acceptable, jobs compute for configured scheduled work, SQL warehouses for BI, and pick access mode by isolation needs.

lessons.title: Databricks Runtime
lessons.summary: The Databricks Runtime (DBR) is the software image on classic compute: Apache Spark plus Databricks improvements, Delta Lake, libraries and system packages.
lessons.remember: DBR packages Spark, Delta and libraries; pin LTS versions on classic compute and let serverless upgrade itself.

lessons.title: Photon
lessons.summary: Photon is Databricks' native, vectorised query engine written in C++.
lessons.remember: Photon is a C++ vectorised engine under Spark's planner that speeds up SQL and DataFrame work, but not UDFs, RDDs or stateful streaming.

lessons.title: Unity Catalog: metastore, catalogs and schemas
lessons.summary: Unity Catalog (UC) is Databricks' governance layer.
lessons.remember: Unity Catalog governs everything through metastore, catalog, schema and object, addressed as catalog.schema.table.

lessons.title: Privileges and ownership
lessons.summary: Access in Unity Catalog is granted with SQL GRANT on securables to users, groups and service principals: - Reading a table needs USE CATALOG on its catalog, USE SCHEMA on its schema and SELECT on the table.
lessons.remember: Reading needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT; grants inherit downward, and ABAC policies on governed tags scale row and column protection.

lessons.title: Lineage in Unity Catalog
lessons.summary: Unity Catalog captures lineage automatically for queries run on UC-enabled compute: table-level and column-level, across all workspaces attached to the metastore, for notebooks, jobs, pipelines, dashboards and models.
lessons.remember: Unity Catalog records table and column lineage automatically for governed queries, visible in Catalog Explorer and system tables.

lessons.title: Volumes
lessons.summary: A volume is a Unity Catalog object that governs non-tabular files: CSV drops, JSON, images, PDFs, model artefacts, libraries.
lessons.remember: Volumes bring governed paths and permissions to files that are not tables.

lessons.title: Storage credentials and external locations
lessons.summary: Unity Catalog controls how Databricks reaches cloud storage with two objects: - A storage credential wraps a cloud identity (an Azure managed identity or service principal, an AWS IAM role, a GCP service account) that ca
lessons.remember: Storage credentials hold the cloud identity, external locations bind it to paths, and UC privileges decide who may use them.

lessons.title: System tables
lessons.summary: System tables are read-only tables in the system catalog that expose operational data about your account as data you can query: - system.access.audit: who did what (logins, queries, permission changes).
lessons.remember: System tables expose audit, lineage, billing, compute and job history as queryable tables.

lessons.title: Delta Sharing (OpenSharing)
lessons.summary: Delta Sharing is an open protocol, created by Databricks, for sharing live data without copying it.
lessons.remember: Delta Sharing (now OpenSharing) shares live, read-only data across organisations and platforms without copying it.

lessons.title: Notebooks and the workspace
lessons.summary: Databricks notebooks mix Python, SQL, Scala and R cells (by default one language per notebook, with magic commands to switch), run on attached compute, and show results, charts and Spark job progress inline.
lessons.remember: Notebooks are for exploration and orchestration of steps; with Git folders they become versioned code, but shared logic belongs in modules.

lessons.title: Jobs (Lakeflow Jobs)
lessons.summary: Lakeflow Jobs (formerly Databricks Jobs, then Workflows) is Databricks' built-in orchestrator.
lessons.remember: Lakeflow Jobs orchestrates multi-task workflows on Databricks with triggers, retries, branching and repair runs.

lessons.title: Declarative pipelines (formerly Delta Live Tables)
lessons.summary: Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines (the product formerly called Delta Live Tables, renamed in stages during 2025; Databricks pages also say "Spark Declarative Pipelines on Lakeflow") let you declare what tables should
lessons.remember: Declarative pipelines (formerly DLT) define streaming tables and materialized views with expectations and AUTO CDC, and Databricks runs the rest.

lessons.title: Auto Loader
lessons.summary: Auto Loader is Databricks' incremental file ingestion source (cloudFiles) for Structured Streaming and declarative pipelines.
lessons.remember: Auto Loader loads new files exactly once with scalable discovery, schema inference and controlled schema evolution.

lessons.title: Managed ingestion connectors (Lakeflow Connect)
lessons.summary: Lakeflow Connect provides managed connectors that ingest data into Unity Catalog tables without writing pipeline code: - SaaS connectors such as Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, Google Analytics, Microsoft Dynamics 365,
lessons.remember: Lakeflow Connect is Databricks' managed ingestion for SaaS apps and databases, landing data as governed streaming tables.

lessons.title: Medallion architecture on Databricks
lessons.summary: On Databricks the medallion layers are usually mapped onto Unity Catalog and Lakeflow: - Catalogs per environment (dev, prod) and sometimes per domain; schemas per layer (bronze, silver, gold), or catalogs per layer in l
lessons.remember: On Databricks, medallion layers become catalogs or schemas fed by declarative pipelines, with UC grants per layer.

lessons.title: Delta optimisations on Databricks
lessons.summary: On top of open-source Delta, Databricks adds features that keep tables fast with little manual work: - OPTIMIZE compacts small files (and clusters data when clustering is defined).
lessons.remember: Databricks keeps Delta tables fast with optimized writes, auto compaction, deletion vectors and data skipping, most automatic on managed tables.

lessons.title: Liquid clustering
lessons.summary: Liquid clustering organises a Delta table's data by up to four clustering keys (CLUSTER BY (customerid, eventdate)) so that queries filtering on those keys skip most files.
lessons.remember: Liquid clustering replaces partitioning and Z-order with incremental, changeable clustering keys, chosen automatically if you let it.

lessons.title: Predictive optimization
lessons.summary: Predictive optimization runs table maintenance automatically on Unity Catalog managed tables: OPTIMIZE (compaction and clustering), VACUUM (removing old files) and ANALYZE (statistics).
lessons.remember: Predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE for you on managed tables, billed as serverless usage.

lessons.title: SQL warehouses
lessons.summary: A SQL warehouse is Databricks compute dedicated to SQL: the SQL editor, dashboards, Genie, BI tools (Power BI, Tableau) and JDBC/ODBC clients.
lessons.remember: SQL warehouses are Databricks' SQL compute for BI; prefer serverless, scale up for heavy queries and out for concurrency.

lessons.title: AI/BI dashboards
lessons.summary: AI/BI dashboards are Databricks' built-in dashboards: datasets defined by SQL over Unity Catalog tables, visualisations (with AI help to create charts), filters and cross-filtering, schedules and subscriptions, and embed
lessons.remember: AI/BI dashboards give quick governed dashboards on Databricks; enterprise BI still often lives in Power BI or Tableau.

lessons.title: Genie and natural-language analytics
lessons.summary: Genie is Databricks' natural-language analytics.
lessons.remember: Genie answers business questions by generating SQL over a curated, governed set of tables and metrics; curation decides accuracy.

lessons.title: MLflow on Databricks
lessons.summary: Databricks runs a managed MLflow (MLflow 3 since mid-2025) integrated with the workspace and Unity Catalog: - Experiments track training runs from notebooks and jobs, with autologging for common libraries.
lessons.remember: On Databricks, MLflow tracks experiments and registers models in Unity Catalog with versions, aliases, permissions and lineage.

lessons.title: Feature engineering in Unity Catalog
lessons.summary: In Databricks, any Delta table with a primary key in Unity Catalog can be a feature table.
lessons.remember: On Databricks, feature tables are UC Delta tables with primary keys, joined point-in-time for training and published to a Lakebase-backed online store for serving.

lessons.title: Model serving
lessons.summary: Model Serving deploys models as serverless REST endpoints that scale automatically (including to zero).
lessons.remember: Model Serving hosts custom models, foundation models and external model proxies as serverless endpoints, governed through a gateway.

lessons.title: Vector search
lessons.summary: Databricks' vector search (renamed AI Search in June 2026) maintains vector indexes over Unity Catalog data: - Delta Sync indexes stay in sync with a source Delta table (which needs change data feed).
lessons.remember: Databricks vector search (now AI Search) keeps vector and hybrid indexes in sync with Delta tables for RAG.

lessons.title: Agent tooling
lessons.summary: Databricks groups its agent capabilities under Agent Bricks (names changed repeatedly in 2025-2026; earlier terms include Mosaic AI Agent Framework).
lessons.remember: Databricks agent tooling (Agent Bricks) builds agents on Unity Catalog tools, evaluates them with MLflow traces and judges, and serves them through Model Serving.

lessons.title: Databricks Asset Bundles
lessons.summary: Bundles (introduced as Databricks Asset Bundles; renamed Declarative Automation Bundles in March 2026, with the bundle command and "DAB" abbreviation unchanged) define a Databricks project as code.
lessons.remember: Bundles declare a project's jobs, pipelines and other resources in YAML with per-environment targets, deployed by the CLI.

lessons.title: Terraform for Databricks
lessons.summary: The Databricks Terraform provider manages the platform layer as code: workspaces (together with cloud provider resources such as networks and storage), Unity Catalog metastores, catalogs, schemas, storage credentials, ex
lessons.remember: Use the Databricks Terraform provider for workspaces, Unity Catalog objects and permissions; leave project jobs and pipelines to bundles.

lessons.title: CI/CD on Databricks
lessons.summary: Databricks' recommended CI/CD flow: 1.
lessons.remember: Develop in your own bundle target, test in CI, and let service principals deploy bundles to test and prod with approvals.

lessons.title: Compute policies
lessons.summary: Compute policies (formerly cluster policies) are rules that limit what classic compute users can create: allowed node types, maximum workers, required auto-termination, fixed runtime versions, mandatory tags for cost all
lessons.remember: Compute policies constrain classic cluster settings per group to control cost, tagging and security.

lessons.title: Monitoring and observability
lessons.summary: Databricks monitoring spans several tools: - Jobs and pipelines UI: run history, task durations, failures, repair runs, pipeline event logs with data quality metrics.
lessons.remember: Monitor Databricks with job and pipeline UIs, system tables for usage and cost, and data quality monitoring for table health.

lessons.title: DBUs and the cost model
lessons.summary: Databricks charges in Databricks Units (DBUs), a unit of processing capacity per hour, billed per second.
lessons.remember: DBU rates depend on the compute product; classic adds a separate cloud bill while serverless includes infrastructure, and system tables show where spend goes.

lessons.title: When Databricks is the right choice
lessons.summary: Seen from the Databricks side (the full three-way comparison is in the Fabric track), Databricks tends to fit when: - Engineering and data science are central: complex Spark pipelines, streaming, ML training and AI appli
lessons.remember: Choose Databricks when code-heavy engineering, streaming, ML and AI on open formats across clouds are central.

lessons.title: Serverless vs classic compute
lessons.summary: Databricks increasingly defaults to serverless.
lessons.remember: Serverless trades configuration for speed and no infrastructure work; keep classic for code, networking or hardware that serverless cannot handle.

lessons.title: Governance patterns on Databricks
lessons.summary: Common Unity Catalog patterns used by organisations in 2026: - Catalog per environment (dev, test, prod), sometimes combined with catalog per domain (financeprod, salesprod), with schemas for layers or data products.
lessons.remember: Separate catalogs by environment and domain, bind them to the right workspaces, prefer managed tables, grant to groups, and protect sensitive data with tag-based policies.

lessons.title: Storage, compute and cloud services
lessons.summary: Snowflake is a fully managed SaaS data platform built from three independent layers: 1.
lessons.remember: Snowflake separates storage, compute warehouses and a cloud services brain, so many workloads share data without competing.

lessons.title: Virtual warehouses
lessons.summary: A virtual warehouse is a named compute cluster.
lessons.remember: A virtual warehouse is per-second-billed compute that doubles in size and credits per step and suspends when idle.

lessons.title: Micro-partitions
lessons.summary: Snowflake automatically divides every table into micro-partitions: immutable, columnar storage units holding about 50 to 500 MB of uncompressed data, created in the order data is inserted or loaded.
lessons.remember: Snowflake splits tables into small immutable micro-partitions with min and max metadata, and skips those that cannot match a filter.

lessons.title: Editions
lessons.summary: Snowflake is sold in editions; each includes everything in the one before: - Standard: core platform, Time Travel up to 1 day, Fail-safe, secure data sharing.
lessons.remember: Enterprise adds multi-cluster, long Time Travel and masking and row policies; Business Critical adds private connectivity, customer keys and failover.

lessons.title: Credits and billing
lessons.summary: Snowflake bills in credits (with a price per credit set by edition, region and contract) plus storage and data transfer: - Warehouse compute: credits per hour by size, billed per second (60-second minimum per start).
lessons.remember: Snowflake bills credits for warehouses and serverless features, plus storage and egress; serverless features are the cost most often overlooked.

lessons.title: Stages and COPY INTO
lessons.summary: A stage is a location of files Snowflake can load from or unload to: - Internal stages: storage managed by Snowflake: a per-user stage (@~), a per-table stage (@%table), or named internal stages.
lessons.remember: Stages point at files and COPY INTO bulk-loads them in parallel, remembering loaded files for 64 days.

lessons.title: Snowpipe
lessons.summary: Snowpipe loads files continuously as they arrive.
lessons.remember: Snowpipe auto-ingests new files from cloud storage with serverless COPY, billed per GB.

lessons.title: Snowpipe Streaming
lessons.summary: Snowpipe Streaming writes rows directly into Snowflake tables through an SDK or REST API, without staging files first.
lessons.remember: Snowpipe Streaming writes rows straight into tables with seconds of latency, from SDKs, REST or the Kafka connector.

lessons.title: Streams and tasks
lessons.summary: Two building blocks for in-database pipelines: - A stream records changes to a table (or view, dynamic table or Iceberg table) since the stream was last consumed.
lessons.remember: Streams track changed rows since last consumption, and tasks run SQL on schedules or when streams have data.

lessons.title: Dynamic tables
lessons.summary: A dynamic table is defined by a query and a target lag (for example TARGETLAG = '10 minutes', minimum 60 seconds, or DOWNSTREAM).
lessons.remember: A dynamic table is a SQL query plus a target lag; Snowflake keeps it fresh, incrementally where possible.

lessons.title: External tables
lessons.summary: An external table lets Snowflake query files in an external stage (S3, Azure, GCS) without loading them.
lessons.remember: External tables query lake files in place, read-only and slower; Iceberg tables are the modern choice for shared lake data.

lessons.title: Apache Iceberg tables in Snowflake
lessons.summary: Iceberg tables store data as Parquet files with Iceberg metadata in storage you can choose, so other engines (Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB) can read the same tables.
lessons.remember: Snowflake Iceberg tables keep data in open Parquet and Iceberg metadata, managed by Snowflake or an external catalog, readable by other engines.

lessons.title: Caching layers
lessons.summary: Snowflake has three caches: - Result cache (cloud services layer): the result of a query is kept for 24 hours (extended each time it is reused, up to 31 days).
lessons.remember: The result cache returns identical queries free for 24 hours, the warehouse cache keeps recent data local until suspend, and metadata answers simple aggregates.

lessons.title: Clustering keys and automatic clustering
lessons.summary: Natural clustering (data stored in load order) works well when queries filter on the load order, typically date.
lessons.remember: Clustering keys plus Automatic Clustering restore pruning on very large tables, at a continuing serverless and storage cost.

lessons.title: Search optimization service
lessons.summary: The search optimization service (Enterprise Edition) builds and maintains a persistent search access path for chosen tables or columns.
lessons.remember: Search optimization accelerates selective point lookups and searches on large tables, at extra storage and maintenance cost.

lessons.title: Query acceleration service
lessons.summary: The query acceleration service (QAS) (Enterprise Edition) lets a warehouse offload parts of eligible queries, mainly large scans with selective filters or aggregations, to additional serverless compute.
lessons.remember: QAS offloads parts of big scan-heavy queries to serverless compute so a warehouse can handle outliers without upsizing.

lessons.title: Warehouse sizing and multi-cluster warehouses
lessons.summary: Two different scaling problems need two different tools: - Scale up (a bigger warehouse size) when single queries are slow, spill to storage or process lots of data.
lessons.remember: Scale up for heavy single queries, scale out with multi-cluster warehouses for concurrency, and separate warehouses by workload.

lessons.title: Query profile
lessons.summary: The Query Profile in Snowsight shows how a query executed: a graph of operators (TableScan, Filter, Join, Aggregate, Sort) with the time and rows of each, plus statistics.
lessons.remember: In the Query Profile, check pruning, spilling and exploding joins first; they explain most slow Snowflake queries.

lessons.title: Semi-structured data and VARIANT
lessons.summary: Snowflake stores semi-structured data (JSON, Avro, ORC, Parquet, XML) in the VARIANT type, alongside ARRAY and OBJECT.
lessons.remember: VARIANT stores JSON-like data natively; use path notation and FLATTEN to query it, and promote important fields to typed columns.

lessons.title: Time Travel and Fail-safe
lessons.summary: Snowflake keeps historical data in two stages after changes or drops: - Time Travel: you can query data as it was at a past time or before a statement (SELECT ...
lessons.remember: Time Travel lets you query and restore past data for up to 90 days; Fail-safe adds 7 days that only Snowflake Support can recover from.

lessons.title: Zero-copy cloning
lessons.summary: CREATE TABLE devorders CLONE orders (and the same for schemas and databases) creates a clone instantly, without copying data: the clone initially points to the same micro-partitions as the source.
lessons.remember: Cloning creates instant copies that share storage until changes diverge, ideal for test environments and snapshots.

lessons.title: Snowpark
lessons.summary: Snowpark lets you write data logic in Python, Java or Scala that runs inside Snowflake: - A DataFrame API (similar to PySpark) that is translated to SQL and executed lazily by warehouses, so data does not leave Snowflake
lessons.remember: Snowpark runs Python, Java and Scala DataFrames, UDFs and procedures inside Snowflake, so data stays put.

lessons.title: Secure data sharing
lessons.summary: Secure data sharing lets a provider account give other Snowflake accounts read access to live tables, secure views and other objects without copying data.
lessons.remember: Snowflake shares live data between accounts without copies; consumers query it with their own compute.

lessons.title: Snowflake Marketplace
lessons.summary: The Snowflake Marketplace is a catalogue of listings from data providers (market data, weather, demographics, reference data, enrichment services) and of Snowflake Native Apps, applications that run inside the consumer's
lessons.remember: The Marketplace delivers third-party data and native apps as live shares and in-account applications.

lessons.title: Data clean rooms
lessons.summary: A data clean room lets two or more organisations analyse their combined data without either seeing the other's raw records.
lessons.remember: A clean room allows joint analysis on combined data while each party's raw records stay hidden, enforced by templates and policies.

lessons.title: Role-based access control
lessons.summary: Snowflake combines role-based access control (privileges are granted to roles, and roles to users) with discretionary access control (every object has an owner role that can grant on it).
lessons.remember: Snowflake grants privileges to roles in a hierarchy, with owners able to grant; use functional and access roles, future grants and managed access schemas.

lessons.title: Dynamic data masking
lessons.summary: A masking policy (Enterprise Edition) is a schema-level object containing a SQL expression that decides, at query time, what a user sees in a column.
lessons.remember: Masking policies decide per role at query time what a column shows, and tag-based masking applies them automatically wherever a tag appears.

lessons.title: Row access policies
lessons.summary: A row access policy (Enterprise Edition) is an object with a boolean SQL expression evaluated for each row, using the current role or user.
lessons.remember: Row access policies filter rows per role at query time, often via a small mapping table, so one table serves many audiences.

lessons.title: Object tags and data classification
lessons.summary: Object tags are key-value labels (for example pii = 'email', costcenter = 'finance') attached to accounts, warehouses, databases, schemas, tables and columns.
lessons.remember: Tags label objects and columns, classification suggests sensitive-data tags automatically, and tag-based policies protect what is tagged.

lessons.title: Network policies and private connectivity
lessons.summary: Snowflake is reachable over the internet by default.
lessons.remember: Restrict Snowflake with network rules and policies, use private connectivity on Business Critical, and use MFA or key-based service authentication.

lessons.title: Snowflake Horizon
lessons.summary: Snowflake Horizon Catalog is the name Snowflake uses for its built-in governance and discovery capabilities, grouped in one place: - Compliance and security: access control, masking and row access policies, tags and clas
lessons.remember: Horizon is Snowflake's built-in governance, discovery and Iceberg catalog layer, spanning policies, lineage, quality and security posture.

lessons.title: Cortex AI features
lessons.summary: Snowflake Cortex is Snowflake's set of AI services running inside the platform: - Cortex AI Functions (also called AISQL): SQL functions that call large language models on table data: AICOMPLETE, AICLASSIFY, AIFILTER, AI
lessons.remember: Cortex brings LLM functions to SQL, plus managed search, text-to-SQL over semantic views, and agents, all inside Snowflake.

lessons.title: Snowflake ML
lessons.summary: Snowflake ML is the set of tools for the machine learning lifecycle on Snowflake: - Feature Store: feature views over Snowflake tables, with point-in-time lookups for training (an online store was in preview in 2026).
lessons.remember: Snowflake ML provides feature store, container-based training, experiment tracking, registry and serving inside Snowflake's governance.

lessons.title: Snowflake Notebooks
lessons.summary: Snowflake Notebooks run Python, SQL and Markdown cells inside Snowflake.
lessons.remember: Snowflake Notebooks run Python and SQL next to the data, with container runtimes and Git-backed workspaces.

lessons.title: Resource monitors and cost control
lessons.summary: Snowflake gives several cost controls: - Resource monitors track warehouse credit use over a period against a quota, and can notify, suspend after running queries finish, or suspend immediately at thresholds (for example
lessons.remember: Resource monitors cap warehouse credits, budgets cover everything including serverless and AI, and tags plus usage views enable chargeback.

lessons.title: CI/CD and change management for Snowflake
lessons.summary: Options for managing Snowflake objects as code: - Git integration: Snowflake can connect to Git repositories and run files from them.
lessons.remember: Manage Snowflake as code with Git, the CLI, DCM Projects, dbt and Terraform, and test changes on zero-copy clones.

lessons.title: Snowflake vs Databricks vs Fabric
lessons.summary: From the Snowflake side (the full comparison lives in the Fabric track), Snowflake tends to fit when: - The core users are SQL analysts and engineers who want a warehouse that needs almost no administration.
lessons.remember: Snowflake fits SQL-first, low-administration, sharing-heavy and multi-cloud needs, and increasingly interoperates through Iceberg.

lessons.title: Iceberg interoperability
lessons.summary: Snowflake uses Apache Iceberg to work with other engines in both directions: - Other engines reading Snowflake data: Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables are exposed through the Horizon Catalog Iceberg REST endpoint (built o
lessons.remember: Snowflake shares Iceberg tables through its Horizon REST catalog and reads other platforms' Iceberg catalogs, including Unity Catalog and OneLake.

lessons.title: NULL and three-valued logic
lessons.summary: In SQL, NULL means "unknown".
lessons.remember: NULL comparisons are UNKNOWN and filtered out; use IS NULL, NOT EXISTS and null-safe comparison, and remember Oracle's empty string is NULL.

lessons.title: Logical query processing order
lessons.summary: SQL is written in one order but evaluated logically in another: 1.
lessons.remember: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, then TOP or LIMIT: this logical order explains alias and window-function rules.

lessons.title: Join semantics
lessons.summary: - INNER JOIN keeps pairs of rows where the ON condition is TRUE.
lessons.remember: Put outer-join filters in ON, and check key uniqueness before trusting sums after a join.

lessons.title: Set operations
lessons.summary: Set operators combine results of queries with the same number of columns and compatible types, matched by position: - UNION ALL: all rows from both, duplicates kept.
lessons.remember: Prefer UNION ALL unless duplicates must go, match columns by position carefully, and use EXCEPT both ways to diff tables.

lessons.title: Semi joins and anti joins
lessons.summary: A semi join returns rows from the left table that have at least one match on the right, without duplicating them and without adding right-side columns.
lessons.remember: Use EXISTS for "has a match" and NOT EXISTS for "has no match"; NOT IN breaks when NULLs appear.

lessons.title: APPLY and LATERAL
lessons.summary: A normal join combines two independent tables.
lessons.remember: APPLY and LATERAL run a correlated subquery per left row, ideal for top-N-per-row and per-row table functions.

lessons.title: Non-equi joins and self joins
lessons.summary: A non-equi join uses a condition other than equality: ranges (BETWEEN), inequalities, or overlaps.
lessons.remember: Non-equi joins express ranges and overlaps; include an equality key, use half-open intervals, and prefer LAG over self joins for previous-row logic.

lessons.title: Window frames: ROWS vs RANGE
lessons.summary: A window function computes a value per row over a window of related rows: function() OVER (PARTITION BY ...
lessons.remember: Always state ROWS frames for running calculations; the default RANGE frame groups ties and surprises people.

lessons.title: Ranking functions
lessons.summary: Four ranking functions, differing in how they treat ties (rows with equal ORDER BY values): Value order ROWNUMBER RANK DENSERANK ------------ 100 1 1 1 90 2 2 2 90 3 2 2 80 4 4 3 - ROWNUMBER(): unique sequential numbers;
lessons.remember: ROWNUMBER is unique, RANK leaves gaps after ties, DENSERANK does not; pick the one that matches the business meaning of ties.

lessons.title: LAG, LEAD and running totals
lessons.summary: Offset functions read values from other rows in the same partition: - LAG(col, n, default): value from n rows before (default 1).
lessons.remember: LAG and LEAD compare a row with its neighbours, and framed SUMs give running totals, all in one pass.

lessons.title: Gaps and islands
lessons.summary: An island is a run of consecutive values (consecutive days a user was active, consecutive months a contract was valid, consecutive sequence numbers); a gap is a missing range between them.
lessons.remember: Value minus ROWNUMBER is constant within a run of consecutive values; group by it to find islands, and use LEAD to find gaps.

lessons.title: Sessionization
lessons.summary: Sessionization groups a user's events into sessions: a new session starts when the gap since the previous event exceeds a threshold (for example 30 minutes).
lessons.remember: Flag a new session when the gap since the previous event exceeds a threshold, then a running sum of flags numbers the sessions.

lessons.title: Common table expressions
lessons.summary: A common table expression (CTE) names a subquery at the start of a statement with WITH name AS (...), so later parts of the query can refer to it by name.
lessons.remember: CTEs name query steps for readability; they are usually inlined, not cached, so reuse can mean recomputation.

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs and hierarchies
lessons.summary: A recursive CTE refers to itself.
lessons.remember: A recursive CTE starts from anchor rows and repeatedly joins to itself to walk hierarchies; guard against cycles.

lessons.title: Bill of materials and graph traversal
lessons.summary: A bill of materials (BOM) lists the components of a product, each of which may have its own components, with quantities at each level.
lessons.remember: Exploding a BOM multiplies quantities down a recursive CTE; for general graphs carry the path to avoid cycles.

lessons.title: Deduplication
lessons.summary: Duplicates come in two kinds: exact duplicates (every column identical, often from reloading a file twice) and key duplicates (several versions of the same business key with different values).
lessons.remember: Find duplicates with GROUP BY HAVING, keep one per key with ROWNUMBER and a full tie-breaking order, and fix the cause upstream.

lessons.title: Top N per group
lessons.summary: "The three best-selling products per category", "the latest order per customer": three standard solutions: 1.
lessons.remember: Rank within groups and filter (or QUALIFY), or use APPLY with TOP per group when an index supports it.

lessons.title: Pivot and unpivot
lessons.summary: Pivot turns row values into columns (months across the top); unpivot turns columns into rows.
lessons.remember: Conditional aggregation pivots portably, and unpivoting wide legacy tables into rows makes them usable.

lessons.title: Replacing cursors with set-based SQL
lessons.summary: A cursor (or a WHILE loop, or PL/SQL FOR rec IN (SELECT ...) LOOP) processes rows one at a time.
lessons.remember: Replace row-by-row loops with window functions, joins in UPDATE, MERGE and ROWNUMBER; loop over batches, never single rows.

lessons.title: Calendar and date dimension tables
lessons.summary: A calendar table (date dimension) has one row per date, with precomputed attributes: year, quarter, month, week number, day of week, isweekend, isholiday, fiscal year and period, working-day number, and anything else the
lessons.remember: A calendar table precomputes date attributes and fills missing days, making time reporting consistent and simple.

lessons.title: Time series queries
lessons.summary: Common time-series operations in SQL: - Bucketing: truncate timestamps to a period: DATETRUNC('hour', ts) (Snowflake, Spark, Fabric), DATETRUNC(hour, ts) (SQL Server 2022), TRUNC(ts, 'HH24') (Oracle), or DATEBIN for arbi
lessons.remember: Bucket with date truncation, fill gaps from a calendar, compare periods with LAG or calendar joins, and keep timestamps in UTC.

lessons.title: Slowly changing dimensions in SQL
lessons.summary: Dimensions such as customer or product change over time.
lessons.remember: Type 1 overwrites, type 2 expires the old row and inserts a new version with validity dates; facts store the version's surrogate key.

lessons.title: System-versioned temporal tables and flashback
lessons.summary: Databases can keep row history automatically: - SQL Server temporal tables (system-versioned, SQL Server 2016+, Azure SQL): the table has ValidFrom/ValidTo period columns and a linked history table.
lessons.remember: Temporal tables and flashback keep system-time history automatically; business-effective history still needs dimensional modelling.

lessons.title: JSON in SQL
lessons.summary: Every major engine can query JSON, with different syntax: Task T-SQL Oracle Snowflake Spark SQL --------------- Storage type NVARCHAR(MAX), native json type (2025, verify) JSON type (21c+) or text with IS JSON VARIANT ST
lessons.remember: All engines parse JSON with path functions and explode arrays into rows (OPENJSON, JSONTABLE, FLATTEN, explode); extract hot fields into columns.

lessons.title: XML in SQL
lessons.summary: Legacy integrations (SOAP services, banking and insurance messages, older ERP exports) still produce XML.
lessons.remember: Shred XML into rows with nodes() and value() in SQL Server or XMLTABLE in Oracle, declare namespaces, and do it once at load.

lessons.title: MERGE and upserts
lessons.summary: MERGE (T-SQL, Oracle, Snowflake, Spark SQL with Delta, Fabric Warehouse) compares a source with a target on a key and, in one statement, updates matched rows, inserts unmatched source rows, and (in T-SQL, Snowflake and D
lessons.remember: MERGE upserts and optionally deletes in one atomic statement; deduplicate the source, update only real changes, and mind SQL Server's concurrency caveats.

lessons.title: Bulk operations
lessons.summary: Loading or changing millions of rows needs different techniques from single-row DML: - Bulk load: SQL Server BULK INSERT, bcp and SqlBulkCopy; Oracle SQLLoader, external tables and direct-path INSERT /+ APPEND /; Snowfla
lessons.remember: Use bulk loaders, minimal logging where acceptable, batched deletes and partition switching instead of row-by-row DML.

lessons.title: Transactions and isolation levels
lessons.summary: A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail together (ACID: atomic, consistent, isolated, durable).
lessons.remember: Isolation levels trade consistency for concurrency; Oracle and RCSI use row versions so readers do not block writers, and NOLOCK can return wrong data.

lessons.title: Locking, blocking and deadlocks
lessons.summary: Databases lock data to keep transactions isolated.
lessons.remember: Blocking is waiting, deadlock is a cycle the engine breaks by killing one side; keep transactions short, ordered and indexed, and retry victims.

lessons.title: Execution plans
lessons.summary: An execution plan shows how the optimiser decided to run a query: which indexes, which join algorithms, in what order, with estimated and actual row counts.
lessons.remember: Read the actual plan and compare estimated with actual rows first; mismatches, scans and spills point to the cause.

lessons.title: Index types
lessons.summary: Indexes are additional structures that let the engine find rows without scanning the whole table.
lessons.remember: Clustered and nonclustered B-trees serve OLTP lookups, columnstore and bitmap serve analytics, and cloud warehouses replace indexes with pruning.

lessons.title: Statistics and cardinality estimation
