lessons.summary: The optimiser chooses plans from estimates of how many rows each step returns (cardinality).
lessons.remember: The optimiser plans from statistics; refresh them after big loads and add histograms or extended stats for skewed or correlated data.

lessons.title: Sargability
lessons.summary: A predicate is sargable (Search ARGument ABLE) when the engine can use an index seek or partition pruning to evaluate it.
lessons.remember: Keep the column bare on one side of the predicate; move functions and arithmetic to the constant side, and match data types.

lessons.title: Parameter sniffing
lessons.summary: SQL Server compiles a stored procedure or parameterised query once and caches the plan, optimised for the parameter values used at first compilation ("sniffed").
lessons.remember: Cached plans fit the first parameter values; with skewed data use recompile hints, Query Store forcing or PSP optimisation (Oracle: adaptive cursor sharing).

lessons.title: Table partitioning
lessons.summary: Partitioning splits one logical table into physical pieces by a key, usually date: - SQL Server: a partition function defines boundary values and a partition scheme maps partitions to filegroups; tables and indexes are c
lessons.remember: Partition big tables by date for elimination and sliding-window loads and purges; it is mainly for manageability, not lookups.

lessons.title: Query hints
lessons.summary: Hints override optimiser decisions: - SQL Server: table hints (WITH (INDEX(ixname)), FORCESEEK), join hints (LOOP, HASH, MERGE), and query hints with OPTION (...) such as RECOMPILE, MAXDOP n, OPTIMIZE FOR, USE HINT('...'
lessons.remember: Hints override the optimiser for proven problems; they age badly, so prefer statistics, indexing and plan management.

lessons.title: Stored procedures and packages
lessons.summary: A stored procedure is named code stored and executed in the database, with parameters, variables, control flow, transactions and error handling.
lessons.remember: Procedures and PL/SQL packages keep logic in the database behind a stable interface; in migrations, translate set-based ones and redesign procedural ones.

lessons.title: User-defined functions
lessons.summary: User-defined functions (UDFs) return a value or a table and can be used inside queries: - Scalar functions return one value per call.
lessons.remember: Prefer inline table-valued or inlinable functions; scalar and multi-statement functions can quietly destroy performance.

lessons.title: Triggers
lessons.summary: A trigger is code that runs automatically when data changes (DML triggers on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) or on schema events (DDL triggers).
lessons.remember: Triggers run automatically on data changes but hide cost and logic; prefer temporal tables, CDC and constraints, and plan replacements when migrating.

lessons.title: Dynamic SQL and SQL injection
lessons.summary: Dynamic SQL builds statement text at runtime and executes it: spexecutesql or EXEC in T-SQL, EXECUTE IMMEDIATE and DBMSSQL in Oracle, EXECUTE IMMEDIATE in Snowflake.
lessons.remember: Bind values as parameters, whitelist and quote identifiers, and never concatenate user input into SQL.

lessons.title: Error handling
lessons.summary: Robust database code catches errors, rolls back incomplete work, and reports clearly.
lessons.remember: Catch, roll back, log, then re-raise; never swallow errors, and use XACTABORT ON in T-SQL transactions.

lessons.title: Cohorts and retention
lessons.summary: A cohort is a group of users (or customers, accounts) who started in the same period, for example everyone whose first purchase was in March 2025.
lessons.remember: Group users by start period, count who is active in each following period, and divide by cohort size.

lessons.title: Funnels
lessons.summary: A funnel measures how many users pass through ordered steps, for example: viewed product, added to cart, started checkout, paid.
lessons.remember: Take each user's first time at each step, require increasing times, and compare step counts.

lessons.title: Percentiles and medians
lessons.summary: Averages hide skew: a few large orders inflate the mean.
lessons.remember: Use medians and percentiles for skewed data, approximate versions at scale, and never average them across groups.

lessons.title: A/B test analysis in SQL
lessons.summary: In an A/B test, users are randomly assigned to a control (A) and a variant (B), and a metric (conversion, revenue per user) is compared.
lessons.remember: SQL prepares A/B data (one row per assigned user, outcome in window, sample ratio check); the inference needs proper statistics.

lessons.title: Reconciliation queries
lessons.summary: During a migration, reconciliation proves the new system holds the same data and produces the same results as the old one.
lessons.remember: Compare counts, then aggregates, then partition checksums, then row diffs where checksums differ, after normalising values.

lessons.title: Translating between Oracle, T-SQL, Spark SQL and Snowflake
lessons.summary: Most SQL translates directly; the differences cluster in a few areas: Area Oracle T-SQL Spark SQL Snowflake --------------- Row limit FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY, ROWNUM TOP (n), OFFSET/FETCH LIMIT n LIMIT n, TOP n NULL repl
lessons.remember: Syntax converts with tools; behaviour differences (empty strings, dates, division, collation) need deliberate tests.

lessons.title: Data type mapping across platforms
lessons.summary: Type mismatches are a top source of migration bugs.
lessons.remember: Map types deliberately: Oracle NUMBER needs a chosen precision, Oracle DATE has a time, and timestamps need an explicit time-zone decision.

tracks.name: Python for Data, ML and AI

lessons.title: Types, references and mutability
lessons.summary: In Python, variables are names that refer to objects.
lessons.remember: Python names point to objects; mutating a shared mutable object changes it for everyone, so copy deliberately and avoid mutable defaults.

lessons.title: Comprehensions, iterators and generators
lessons.summary: - Comprehensions build lists, dicts and sets concisely: f(x) for x in rows if cond(x), {k: v for k, v in pairs}.
lessons.remember: Comprehensions build collections concisely; generators stream values lazily so large data never has to fit in memory.

lessons.title: Functions, closures and decorators
lessons.summary: Functions in Python are objects: they can be passed as arguments, returned from other functions and stored in variables.
lessons.remember: Functions are objects; decorators wrap them to add behaviour, and most data frameworks are built on that idea.

lessons.title: Classes and dataclasses
lessons.summary: A class bundles data (attributes) with behaviour (methods).
lessons.remember: Use dataclasses for typed records and config, Pydantic to validate external input, and keep transformation logic in functions.

lessons.title: Exceptions and context managers
lessons.summary: - Exceptions: try / except SpecificError / else / finally.
lessons.remember: Catch specific errors, add context and re-raise; use with blocks so connections, files and transactions are always cleaned up.

lessons.title: Type hints
lessons.summary: Type hints annotate the expected types of variables, parameters and return values: def load(path: str, limit: int None = None) - pd.DataFrame:.
lessons.remember: Type hints document and statically check code; libraries like Pydantic and FastAPI also use them at runtime.

lessons.title: Virtual environments and pip
lessons.summary: A virtual environment is an isolated folder with its own Python interpreter link and installed packages, so each project has its own dependency versions.
lessons.remember: One virtual environment per project keeps dependencies isolated and reproducible; never install project packages globally.

lessons.title: uv, Poetry and lock files
lessons.summary: Modern Python projects declare dependencies in pyproject.toml and pin exact resolved versions in a lock file: - Direct dependencies (what you asked for, with version ranges) live in pyproject.toml.
lessons.remember: Declare dependencies in pyproject.toml and pin everything in a lock file; uv makes this fast.

lessons.title: Project layout and packaging
lessons.summary: A maintainable data project follows a standard layout: The src layout prevents accidentally importing code from the working directory instead of the installed package.
lessons.remember: Use a src layout with pyproject.toml, tests beside it, and build a wheel that every environment installs.

lessons.title: NumPy arrays and broadcasting
lessons.summary: NumPy is the foundation of numerical Python.
lessons.remember: NumPy arrays are typed blocks of memory processed in C, and broadcasting combines shapes without loops.

lessons.title: Vectorisation
lessons.summary: Vectorisation means expressing a computation as operations on whole arrays or columns instead of a Python loop over elements.
lessons.remember: Replace Python loops with whole-array operations; the speed comes from running in compiled code once instead of the interpreter per element.

lessons.title: pandas DataFrames and indexing
lessons.summary: pandas is the standard Python library for tabular data on one machine.
lessons.remember: A DataFrame is labelled columns plus an index; select with loc by label and iloc by position, and avoid chained assignment.

lessons.title: groupby, merge and reshaping
lessons.summary: pandas' core relational operations: - groupby follows split-apply-combine: split rows by keys, apply an aggregation or transformation per group, combine results.
lessons.remember: groupby is split-apply-combine, merge is a SQL join (validate the keys), and melt and pivottable reshape between long and wide.

lessons.title: Time series in pandas
lessons.summary: pandas has rich time-series support: - Parse to datetime64 with pd.todatetime (format and utc=True explicit).
lessons.remember: Use a UTC DatetimeIndex, resample to change frequency, rolling for moving windows, and shift for period comparisons.

lessons.title: Memory use in pandas
lessons.summary: pandas DataFrames often use far more memory than the file they came from.
lessons.remember: Shrink pandas memory with correct dtypes, categoricals, Arrow types and reading only needed columns; beyond that, change tools.

lessons.title: pandas vs Polars
lessons.summary: Polars is a DataFrame library written in Rust on Apache Arrow memory.
lessons.remember: Polars is a fast, lazy, expression-based DataFrame library; pandas has the broadest ecosystem.

lessons.title: matplotlib and seaborn
lessons.summary: - matplotlib is Python's foundational plotting library.
lessons.remember: matplotlib draws anything with full control; seaborn makes statistical plots from DataFrames quickly on top of it.

lessons.title: Plotly
lessons.summary: Plotly produces interactive charts (hover, zoom, pan, toggle series) rendered in the browser with JavaScript.
lessons.remember: Plotly makes interactive browser charts from DataFrames, and Dash or Streamlit turn them into data apps.

lessons.title: Choosing a visualisation library
lessons.summary: Pick the tool by audience and lifetime of the chart: Need Good choice ------ Quick look during analysis pandas .plot(), seaborn Static chart for a document or paper matplotlib, seaborn Interactive exploration in a notebo
lessons.remember: Use Python libraries for analysis and small apps, and BI tools for governed reporting used by many people.

lessons.title: Files and formats from Python
lessons.summary: Python reads and writes every common data format: - CSV: pandas.readcsv / polars.readcsv; the standard library csv module for streaming rows.
lessons.remember: pandas, Polars, pyarrow and DuckDB read every format; fsspec reaches cloud storage, and delta-rs and pyiceberg read lakehouse tables without Spark.

lessons.title: Calling REST APIs
lessons.summary: Many sources are SaaS applications exposing REST APIs.
lessons.remember: A good API extractor sets timeouts, handles auth, pages through cursors, backs off on 429s, extracts incrementally and lands raw JSON first.

lessons.title: SQL from Python
lessons.summary: Python talks to databases through DB-API drivers: pyodbc or mssql-python for SQL Server, oracledb for Oracle, psycopg for PostgreSQL, snowflake-connector-python, databricks-sql-connector.
lessons.remember: Use DB-API drivers with bound parameters, SQLAlchemy for engines and portability, and bulk tools rather than tosql for large loads.

lessons.title: Cleaning and EDA workflow
lessons.summary: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is a repeatable routine to understand a new dataset before building on it: 1.
lessons.remember: Check shape, keys, missing values, distributions, categories and relationships, then turn findings into coded cleaning steps and quality rules.

lessons.title: Profiling
lessons.summary: Profiling measures where time and memory actually go, instead of guessing: - cProfile (standard library): counts calls and time per function; view results with snakeviz or pstats.
lessons.remember: Measure with a profiler first; the slow part is rarely where you guess.

lessons.title: Threads, processes and async
lessons.summary: Python offers three ways to do several things at once, suited to different bottlenecks: - Threads (threading, concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor): good for I/O-bound work (API calls, database queries, file downloads),
lessons.remember: Threads or asyncio for waiting on I/O, processes for CPU-bound Python, and vectorised libraries already use multiple cores.

lessons.title: Apache Arrow
lessons.summary: Apache Arrow is a standard in-memory columnar format: a language-independent layout for tables in memory, with typed columns, null bitmaps and efficient strings.
lessons.remember: Arrow is the shared in-memory columnar format that lets Spark, pandas, Polars and DuckDB exchange data without costly conversion.

lessons.title: Configuration and logging
lessons.summary: Configuration: separate what changes per environment (paths, table names, URLs, batch sizes) from code.
lessons.remember: Keep environment settings out of code and validated at startup, and log with levels and context through the logging module.

lessons.title: Testing with pytest
lessons.summary: pytest is the standard Python test framework.
lessons.remember: Write plain-assert pytest tests for transformation functions and edge cases, with fixtures for setup and mocks for external systems.

lessons.title: Git for data work
lessons.summary: Git tracks changes to files as commits, on branches, in a repository that is shared through a remote (GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab).
lessons.remember: Branch, commit small, review through pull requests, and never commit secrets or data.

lessons.title: Docker basics for Python
lessons.summary: A Dockerfile describes how to build an image for a Python application: 1.
lessons.remember: A layered Dockerfile installs pinned dependencies, copies code and runs as non-root, so the tested environment is what runs.

lessons.title: Notebooks vs scripts
lessons.summary: Notebooks (Jupyter, VS Code, Databricks, Fabric, Snowflake) mix code, output, charts and text in cells.
lessons.remember: Explore in notebooks, move logic into tested modules, and keep any production notebook thin.

lessons.title: SciPy and statsmodels
lessons.summary: Two libraries for classical statistics in Python: - SciPy (scipy.stats): probability distributions (normal, binomial, Poisson, and many more) with densities, quantiles and random sampling; hypothesis tests (t-tests, chi-
lessons.remember: SciPy provides distributions and statistical tests; statsmodels fits models with standard errors and confidence intervals.

lessons.title: scikit-learn overview
lessons.summary: scikit-learn is the standard library for classical machine learning on tabular data.
lessons.remember: scikit-learn gives every classical model the same fit and predict API, and pipelines keep preprocessing consistent and leak-free.

lessons.title: PyTorch overview
lessons.summary: PyTorch is the dominant open-source framework for deep learning (Linux Foundation, originally from Meta).
lessons.remember: PyTorch provides GPU tensors, automatic gradients and neural network modules; use it for deep learning, and tree models for most tabular data.

lessons.title: Linear algebra for ML
lessons.summary: Machine learning treats data as numbers arranged in vectors and matrices: - A vector is an ordered list of numbers: one customer's features (age, tenure, spend) or one word's embedding.
lessons.remember: Data is a matrix of rows and features, models multiply features by weights (dot products), and similarity is measured with distances and dot products.

lessons.title: Calculus essentials: derivatives and gradients
lessons.summary: Training a model means adjusting parameters to reduce a loss (an error measure).
lessons.remember: The gradient is the vector of slopes of the loss; stepping against it reduces error, and the chain rule computes it through layers.

lessons.title: Probability
lessons.summary: Probability quantifies uncertainty, and many ML outputs are probabilities.
lessons.remember: Conditional probability and Bayes' rule update beliefs with evidence, and base rates decide how meaningful a positive result is.

lessons.title: Distributions
lessons.summary: A distribution describes how values of a variable are spread.
lessons.remember: Know the shape: normal for symmetric noise, binomial and Poisson for counts, long tails for money and usage, and use medians for skewed data.

lessons.title: Hypothesis testing
lessons.summary: A hypothesis test asks whether an observed difference could plausibly be due to chance.
lessons.remember: A p-value is the chance of data this extreme if nothing were going on; plan power, fix alpha in advance, and report effect sizes.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals
lessons.summary: A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of plausible values for an unknown quantity (a conversion rate, a mean, a model's accuracy) from a sample.
lessons.remember: A confidence interval shows the plausible range of an estimate; width shrinks with the square root of sample size.

lessons.title: Optimisation and gradient descent
lessons.summary: Training a model is optimisation: find parameters that minimise a loss function measuring error on training data, such as mean squared error for regression or log loss (cross-entropy) for classification.
lessons.remember: Training minimises a loss by stepping against the gradient, with the learning rate setting the step size.

lessons.title: Framing an ML problem
lessons.summary: Most ML projects fail at framing, not modelling.
lessons.remember: Frame the decision, the exact target, what is known at prediction time, the metric and the baseline before choosing any model.

lessons.title: Supervised, unsupervised and other learning types
lessons.summary: - Supervised learning: learn from examples with known answers (labels).
lessons.remember: Supervised learns from labelled answers, unsupervised finds structure without labels, and self-supervised creates its own labels at scale.

lessons.title: Bias, variance, overfitting and underfitting
lessons.summary: A model's error on new data comes from two competing sources: - Bias: error from a model too simple to capture the pattern (a straight line through curved data).
lessons.remember: Underfitting is too simple (high bias), overfitting is memorising noise (high variance); compare training and validation error to tell which.

lessons.title: Train, validation and test sets
lessons.summary: To estimate how a model will perform on new data, split the data: - Training set: fit the model.
lessons.remember: Train on one part, tune on another, test once on a third, and split by time or group when the data demands it.

lessons.title: Cross-validation
lessons.summary: k-fold cross-validation splits the training data into k parts (folds, often 5).
lessons.remember: Cross-validation rotates evaluation across folds for a stable estimate; use stratified, group or time-series folds when the data requires.

lessons.title: Classification metrics
lessons.summary: For a binary classifier, the confusion matrix counts true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN) and false negatives (FN).
lessons.remember: Use precision when false alarms are costly, recall when misses are costly, PR AUC for rare classes, and pick the threshold from business costs.

lessons.title: Regression metrics
lessons.summary: For numeric predictions: - MAE (mean absolute error): average absolute error, in the target's units.
lessons.remember: MAE is the typical error, RMSE punishes big misses, MAPE fails near zero, and every metric needs a naive baseline.

lessons.title: Data leakage
lessons.summary: Data leakage happens when information that would not be available at prediction time gets into training, so the model looks excellent in testing and fails in production.
lessons.remember: Use only information available at prediction time, split before preprocessing, and treat suspiciously good results as a leakage alarm.

lessons.title: Linear regression
lessons.summary: Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of features plus an intercept: y = b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + ....
lessons.remember: Linear regression fits a weighted sum of features by least squares; it is the transparent baseline every regression model should beat.

lessons.title: Logistic regression
lessons.summary: Logistic regression is the linear model for classification.
lessons.remember: Logistic regression turns a linear score into a probability with the sigmoid; coefficients change the log-odds, and the threshold is a business choice.

lessons.title: Regularisation: ridge, lasso, elastic net
lessons.summary: Regularisation adds a penalty for large coefficients to the loss, discouraging overly complex models: - Ridge (L2): penalises the sum of squared coefficients; shrinks all coefficients towards zero, handles correlated fea
lessons.remember: Regularisation penalises large weights: ridge shrinks them, lasso zeroes some out, and the strength is tuned by cross-validation.

lessons.title: k-nearest neighbours
lessons.summary: k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) predicts by looking up the k most similar training examples (by a distance such as Euclidean or cosine) and taking a majority vote (classification) or average (regression).
lessons.remember: k-NN predicts from the k most similar examples; scale features and use approximate indexes at scale.

lessons.title: Naive Bayes
lessons.summary: Naive Bayes classifiers apply Bayes' rule to compute the probability of each class given the features, with the "naive" assumption that features are independent given the class.
lessons.remember: Naive Bayes applies Bayes' rule assuming independent features; fast and strong for simple text classification, poorly calibrated.

lessons.title: Decision trees
lessons.summary: A decision tree splits data with a sequence of yes/no questions on features ("tenure < 6 months?", "plan = basic?"), choosing at each step the split that best separates the target (by Gini impurity or entropy for classif
lessons.remember: A decision tree is a learned set of if-then splits; easy to explain, prone to overfitting, and the basis of forests and boosting.

lessons.title: Random forests
lessons.summary: A random forest trains many decision trees, each on a random bootstrap sample of rows (bagging) and considering a random subset of features at each split, then averages their predictions (or takes a majority vote).
lessons.remember: A random forest averages many trees trained on random rows and features, cutting variance for robust, low-tuning performance.

lessons.title: Gradient boosting
lessons.summary: Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially: each new, small tree is trained to correct the errors (the gradient of the loss) of the ensemble so far, and its contribution is scaled by a learning rate.
lessons.remember: Gradient boosting adds small trees that fix previous errors; XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are the go-to models for tabular data.

lessons.title: Support vector machines
lessons.summary: A support vector machine (SVM) finds the boundary between classes with the widest possible margin, defined by the closest training points (the support vectors).
lessons.remember: SVMs find the widest-margin boundary, with kernels for non-linear cases; good for smaller, high-dimensional data, rarely first choice today.

lessons.title: Clustering
lessons.summary: Clustering groups similar items without labels: - k-means: choose k, assign points to the nearest of k centroids, move centroids to the mean, repeat.
lessons.remember: Clustering finds groups without labels; k-means for round clusters, density methods for odd shapes and noise, and usefulness is the real test.

lessons.title: PCA and dimensionality reduction
lessons.summary: Principal component analysis (PCA) finds new axes (principal components) that are combinations of the original features, ordered by how much of the data's variance each explains.
lessons.remember: PCA compresses correlated features into a few components that keep most variance; t-SNE and UMAP are for visualising, not measuring.

lessons.title: Anomaly detection
lessons.summary: Anomaly detection finds unusual records: fraud, equipment faults, data quality problems, security events.
lessons.remember: Start anomaly detection with simple statistical baselines, add Isolation Forest or similar for multivariate cases, and route alerts to people who can judge them.

lessons.title: Time series forecasting
lessons.summary: Forecasting predicts future values of a series (demand, load, revenue).
lessons.remember: Beat the seasonal naive baseline, use statistical models for single series and boosted trees with lag features for many, and backtest over time.

lessons.title: Recommender basics
lessons.summary: Recommender systems suggest items (products, content, next actions) to users: - Content-based: recommend items similar to those a user liked, using item attributes or embeddings.
lessons.remember: Recommenders combine content similarity and collaborative patterns from implicit feedback, handle cold start, and are validated online.

lessons.title: Encoding and scaling features
lessons.summary: Models need numbers.
lessons.remember: One-hot for few categories, target encoding (out of fold) for many, and scale numeric features for distance-based and linear models.

lessons.title: Missing data
lessons.summary: Why values are missing matters: - Missing completely at random: unrelated to anything; dropping or simple imputation is fine.
lessons.remember: Ask why data is missing, impute with training statistics, and add missing indicators because missingness often carries signal.

lessons.title: Imbalanced data
lessons.summary: In fraud, default, failure and churn problems, the positive class can be 1 percent or far less.
lessons.remember: For rare classes, use precision-recall metrics, class weights and a tuned threshold; resample only training data and recalibrate.

lessons.title: Feature engineering and selection
lessons.summary: Feature engineering creates inputs that make the pattern easy to learn, usually from domain knowledge: - Aggregates over time windows: purchases in the last 30 days, average ticket size, days since last login.
lessons.remember: Domain-driven features beat algorithm tweaks; select features inside cross-validation and only from information available at prediction time.

lessons.title: scikit-learn pipelines
lessons.summary: A scikit-learn Pipeline chains preprocessing steps and a model into one estimator.
lessons.remember: Put all preprocessing and the model in one pipeline so it is fitted on training data only and deployed as one object.

lessons.title: Hyperparameter tuning
lessons.summary: Hyperparameters are settings chosen before training (tree depth, learning rate, regularisation strength, number of trees).
lessons.remember: Tune with random or Bayesian search under cross-validation; expect modest gains, and log every trial.

lessons.title: Interpretability and SHAP
lessons.summary: Interpretability explains what a model does: - Global explanations: which features matter overall.
lessons.remember: Use permutation importance for global views and SHAP for per-prediction contributions; they explain the model, not causation.

lessons.title: Probability calibration
lessons.summary: A model is calibrated when its predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: of all cases scored 0.2, about 20 percent are positive.
lessons.remember: Calibrated models say 20 percent and mean it; check with reliability curves and fix with Platt or isotonic calibration on held-out data.

lessons.title: Fairness
lessons.summary: Models can treat groups differently because of biased historical data (past decisions encoded in labels), unrepresentative samples, or proxies for protected attributes (postcode standing in for ethnicity).
lessons.remember: Measure model outcomes per group, choose a fairness definition deliberately with stakeholders, and remember proxies carry bias even without protected attributes.

lessons.title: Neurons, layers and activations
lessons.summary: A neural network is built from layers of simple units.
lessons.remember: A neural network stacks layers of weighted sums with non-linear activations, letting it learn complex features from raw data.

lessons.title: Backpropagation
lessons.summary: Backpropagation is how neural networks compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight: 1.
lessons.remember: Backpropagation applies the chain rule backwards through the network to get every weight's gradient in about one extra pass.

lessons.title: Training loops and regularisation
lessons.summary: Training a neural network runs a loop: - Data is split into mini-batches (for example 32 to 1,024 examples).
lessons.remember: Train in mini-batches over epochs, watch validation loss, and use early stopping, dropout, weight decay and augmentation against overfitting.

lessons.title: PyTorch concepts
lessons.summary: The PyTorch building blocks used in every training script: - Tensors (torch.tensor): arrays with a dtype and device (cpu, cuda); move models and data with .to(device).
lessons.remember: PyTorch is tensors on devices, modules with forward methods, data loaders, and autograd plus an optimiser in a loop.

lessons.title: Experiment tracking
lessons.summary: Experiment tracking records every training run so results can be compared and reproduced: - Parameters: hyperparameters, feature set version, data snapshot or version.
lessons.remember: Log parameters, metrics, artefacts, data version and code version for every run so models can be compared and reproduced.

lessons.title: Model registry
lessons.summary: A model registry is the catalogue of trained models intended for use: - Each model has a name and numbered versions, linked to the run that produced them (parameters, metrics, data, code).
lessons.remember: A model registry versions approved models, marks the serving version with aliases, and links each to its training run and data.

lessons.title: Batch vs online serving
lessons.summary: Two main ways to use a model in production: - Batch scoring: on a schedule, score many records at once and write predictions to a table (nightly churn scores for all customers, weekly demand forecasts).
lessons.remember: Score in batch unless the decision happens in real time; online serving adds endpoints, online features and higher cost.

lessons.title: Drift and model monitoring
lessons.summary: Models degrade because the world changes.
lessons.remember: Monitor input drift, prediction drift and data quality as early warnings, and real performance once labels arrive.

lessons.title: Retraining strategies
lessons.summary: Models need refreshing as data changes.
lessons.remember: Retrain on a schedule or trigger, but always compare against the current champion and roll out gradually with rollback.

lessons.title: Feature stores
lessons.summary: A feature store manages features (inputs to models) as shared, governed data: - Feature definitions written once (for example "customer purchases in the last 30 days") and reused by many models.
lessons.remember: A feature store defines features once, serves point-in-time correct history for training and fresh values online, keeping training and serving consistent.

lessons.title: Testing and reproducibility in ML
lessons.summary: ML code needs the same engineering discipline as any code, plus some extra checks: Reproducibility - Pin library versions and environments (lock files, containers).
lessons.remember: Pin environments, fix seeds and version data, and test features, data, model quality and behaviour before promotion.

lessons.title: ML on Spark, Fabric, Databricks and Snowflake
lessons.summary: How the data platforms support ML (details in each platform track): - Spark MLlib: distributed algorithms (linear models, trees, gradient-boosted trees, ALS, clustering) and pipelines for data too large for one machine.
lessons.remember: Spark scales feature engineering and some algorithms, while Fabric, Databricks and Snowflake each wrap MLflow-style tracking, registries and scoring around governed data.

lessons.title: AI vs ML vs deep learning vs generative AI
lessons.summary: The terms nest inside each other: - Artificial intelligence (AI): the broad goal of making computers perform tasks that seem to need intelligence.
lessons.remember: AI contains ML, ML contains deep learning, and generative AI is deep learning that produces new content.

lessons.title: What LLMs can and cannot do
lessons.summary: Large language models generate text by predicting likely next tokens, after training on vast text and further tuning to follow instructions.
lessons.remember: LLMs excel at language, extraction and code over provided context, and are unreliable for unsupported facts, exact computation and deterministic decisions.

lessons.title: Convolutional neural networks
lessons.summary: A convolutional neural network (CNN) processes grid-like data (images, spectrograms) with convolution layers: small filters slide across the input and detect local patterns, using the same weights at every position.
lessons.remember: CNNs slide shared filters over images to detect local patterns hierarchically, and pretrained CNNs are reused for most practical vision tasks.

lessons.title: Sequence models before transformers
lessons.summary: Text, speech and time series are sequences.
lessons.remember: RNNs and LSTMs read sequences step by step, which limited long-range memory and parallel training; transformers solved both with attention.

lessons.title: Transfer learning
lessons.summary: Transfer learning reuses a model trained on a large, general dataset for a new, often smaller task.
lessons.remember: Start from a pretrained model and adapt it, by extracting features or fine-tuning, to get strong results with little labelled data.

lessons.title: Tokenisation
lessons.summary: Language models do not see characters or words; they see tokens: pieces of text from a fixed vocabulary, typically tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand entries.
lessons.remember: LLMs read and write subword tokens; tokens set cost, context limits and latency, and explain some character-level quirks.

lessons.title: Embeddings
lessons.summary: An embedding is a vector of numbers (commonly a few hundred to a few thousand dimensions) that represents the meaning of a piece of content: a word, sentence, document, image or product.
lessons.remember: Embeddings map content to vectors where nearness means similar meaning; they power semantic search, RAG, clustering and matching.

lessons.title: Attention and the transformer
lessons.summary: The transformer (introduced in "Attention Is All You Need", 2017) is the architecture behind modern language models.
lessons.remember: Transformers use self-attention to relate every token to every other in parallel; decoder-only transformers generate text token by token.

lessons.title: Pretraining, fine-tuning and alignment
lessons.summary: An assistant-style LLM is built in stages: 1.
lessons.remember: Pretraining gives knowledge, instruction tuning gives helpfulness, and preference training gives aligned behaviour; none of them guarantees truth.

lessons.title: Context windows
lessons.summary: The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once: the system prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool definitions and results, plus the output it generates.
lessons.remember: The context window bounds what a model can see, but quality drops as context grows, so supply the smallest relevant context.

lessons.title: Inference parameters
lessons.summary: Settings that control how a model generates output: - Temperature: scales randomness.
lessons.remember: Use low temperature for consistent extraction, cap output tokens, and use reasoning effort only where the task needs it.

lessons.title: Prompting
lessons.summary: A prompt is everything the model receives: a system prompt (role, rules, output format), the user's request, and any supplied context.
lessons.remember: Be specific, give context and examples, separate instructions from data, and measure prompt changes against a test set.

lessons.title: Structured outputs
lessons.summary: Data pipelines need machine-readable output, not prose.
lessons.remember: Structured outputs guarantee schema-valid JSON via constrained decoding; still validate values and allow nulls for missing information.

lessons.title: Tool and function calling
lessons.summary: Tool calling (function calling) lets a model use your code.
lessons.remember: With tool calling, the model proposes a function call and your code runs it and returns the result; you control permissions.

lessons.title: Cost and latency
lessons.summary: LLM cost is mostly tokens: price per million input tokens plus (usually higher) price per million output tokens, including hidden reasoning tokens.
lessons.remember: Cost and latency scale with tokens; right-size the model, cache static prompt prefixes, batch what can wait, and trim context and output.

lessons.title: RAG: retrieval-augmented generation
lessons.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers questions using your own documents.
lessons.remember: RAG retrieves relevant chunks of your documents into the prompt so the model answers from them with citations; retrieval quality decides answer quality.

lessons.title: Chunking and document preparation
lessons.summary: Before retrieval, documents must be parsed and chunked: - Parsing: extract clean text and structure from PDFs, Word, HTML, slides and scans: headings, tables, lists, page numbers.
lessons.remember: Parse documents carefully, chunk along their structure, attach rich metadata, and add context to chunks so each can stand alone.

lessons.title: Vector search and indexes
lessons.summary: Vector search finds the chunks whose embeddings are nearest to the query's embedding.
lessons.remember: Vector search uses approximate indexes such as HNSW to find semantically similar chunks fast, with metadata filters for scope and permissions.

lessons.title: Hybrid search
lessons.summary: Hybrid search runs two retrievers and merges their results: - Keyword (lexical) search, typically BM25: scores documents by matching terms, weighted by rarity.
lessons.remember: Combine BM25 keyword search with vector search, merge with reciprocal rank fusion, and you catch both exact terms and meaning.

lessons.title: Reranking
lessons.summary: Retrievers are built for speed: they encode query and documents separately (a bi-encoder) and compare vectors.
lessons.remember: Retrieve broadly and cheaply, then rerank candidates with a cross-encoder so the best passages reach the model.

lessons.title: Evaluating RAG
lessons.summary: Evaluate the two halves of RAG separately and together: Retrieval - Recall at k: is a relevant chunk among the top k?
lessons.remember: Measure retrieval (recall, ranking) and generation (faithfulness, relevance, correctness) on a fixed question set, using LLM judges checked against humans.

lessons.title: Tool-using agents
lessons.summary: An agent is an LLM that runs in a loop, deciding its own next step: it reads the goal and context, chooses a tool to call (or answers), observes the tool result, and repeats until it decides the task is done or a limit i
lessons.remember: An agent loops: decide, call a tool, observe, repeat; prefer simple workflows unless the task truly needs dynamic steps.

lessons.title: Planning and reasoning patterns
lessons.summary: Common patterns for structuring how an LLM system works through a task: - Prompt chaining: fixed sequence of steps, each output feeding the next, with checks between.
lessons.remember: Use chaining, routing, planning, orchestrator-worker and critique patterns deliberately, choosing the simplest that measurably works.

lessons.title: Agent memory
lessons.summary: LLMs are stateless: each call sees only its context.
lessons.remember: Agents keep short-term memory in the context window and long-term memory in external stores, retrieved selectively and governed like data.

lessons.title: Model Context Protocol
lessons.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data.
lessons.remember: MCP is the open standard for plugging tools and data into AI applications through servers; it standardises connections, not trust.

lessons.title: Multi-agent patterns
lessons.summary: Multi-agent systems split work across several LLM agents with different roles, prompts or tools: - Manager (orchestrator-worker): a central agent delegates sub-tasks to specialist agents (treated as tools) and combines r
lessons.remember: Use multiple agents (manager or handoff patterns) only when one agent cannot cope; they add cost and coordination risk.

lessons.title: Agent failure modes
lessons.summary: Typical ways agents go wrong: - Loops: repeating the same tool call or plan without progress.
lessons.remember: Agents loop, misuse tools, compound errors and can be hijacked; bound them with limits, least privilege, approvals, validation and tracing.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning
lessons.summary: Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on your own examples so its behaviour changes.
lessons.remember: Fine-tune to change behaviour, format or cost on a narrow task with good examples; use retrieval, not fine-tuning, to add knowledge.

lessons.title: LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessons.summary: Full fine-tuning updates every weight of a large model, which needs a lot of GPU memory and produces a full-size copy per task.
lessons.remember: LoRA and QLoRA fine-tune large models by training small add-on matrices, making adaptation cheap and adapters swappable.

lessons.title: Distillation
lessons.summary: Distillation trains a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher.
lessons.remember: Distillation trains a small model on a large model's outputs for one task, cutting cost and latency within the teacher's quality and licence limits.

lessons.title: When not to fine-tune
lessons.summary: Providers and practitioners recommend trying simpler options first, in this order: 1.
lessons.remember: Prompt, constrain, retrieve and switch models before fine-tuning; fine-tune only with an evaluation set showing it helps.

lessons.title: Batch, CDC and streaming ingestion
lessons.summary: There are three basic ways to move data from source systems into an analytics platform: - Batch extraction: copy a full table or the rows changed since a timestamp, on a schedule (hourly, nightly).
lessons.remember: Batch copies snapshots on a schedule, CDC copies every change from the log, and streaming carries events as they happen.

lessons.title: Debezium and log-based CDC
lessons.summary: Debezium is an open-source CDC platform (from Red Hat, Apache 2.0) that reads database change logs and emits one event per row change, with before and after values and source metadata.
lessons.remember: Debezium turns database logs into row-change events for Kafka or other targets, at the cost of running and monitoring it yourself.

lessons.title: Managed connectors: Fivetran, Airbyte and similar
lessons.summary: Managed connector platforms sell pre-built, maintained pipelines from hundreds of sources (SaaS apps such as Salesforce and Workday, databases, files, APIs) into warehouses and lakehouses.
lessons.remember: Managed connectors buy maintained ingestion from many sources; pay attention to row-based pricing and where data flows.

lessons.title: Azure Data Factory
lessons.summary: Azure Data Factory (ADF) is Azure's cloud data integration and orchestration service.
lessons.remember: ADF is Azure's established pipeline and copy service with self-hosted and SSIS runtimes; Fabric Data Factory is its successor for new Fabric-based work.

lessons.title: Apache Kafka
lessons.summary: Apache Kafka is a distributed, durable log for events.
lessons.remember: Kafka is a replicated, partitioned, replayable log; order holds within a partition and consumer groups scale reading.

lessons.title: Azure Event Hubs
lessons.summary: Azure Event Hubs is Azure's managed event ingestion service, with the same core model as Kafka: event hubs (topics) with partitions, consumer groups and retention.
lessons.remember: Event Hubs is Azure's managed event log with a Kafka-compatible endpoint, sized by tier and throughput units.

lessons.title: Amazon Kinesis
lessons.summary: AWS's streaming family: - Kinesis Data Streams: a managed, partitioned stream.
lessons.remember: Kinesis Data Streams is AWS's shard-based event stream, Firehose delivers streams to storage, and managed Flink processes them.

lessons.title: Apache Pulsar
lessons.summary: Apache Pulsar is a messaging and streaming platform that separates serving from storage: stateless brokers handle clients, while data is stored in Apache BookKeeper nodes as segments.
lessons.remember: Pulsar separates brokers from BookKeeper storage and adds native multi-tenancy and geo-replication, but has a smaller ecosystem than Kafka.

lessons.title: Apache Flink vs Spark Structured Streaming
lessons.summary: Both are distributed stream processors with event-time windows, watermarks, state and exactly-once checkpoints, but they come from different designs: - Apache Flink processes record by record as a true streaming engine,
lessons.remember: Choose Flink for millisecond, stateful event processing; choose Spark Structured Streaming when micro-batch latency is enough and you want one engine for batch and streaming.

lessons.title: Schema registries
lessons.summary: A schema registry stores versioned schemas for the messages on a stream.
lessons.remember: A schema registry versions message schemas and rejects incompatible changes before they break consumers.

lessons.title: Parquet and ORC
lessons.summary: Columnar file formats store each column's values together instead of each row's values together.
lessons.remember: Parquet stores columns in row groups with footer statistics, so engines read only needed columns and skip irrelevant chunks.

lessons.title: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi compared
lessons.summary: A table format turns a folder of Parquet files into a table with transactions, schema, history and statistics.
lessons.remember: Delta, Iceberg and Hudi all add transactions to Parquet; Iceberg is the most engine-neutral, Delta leads in Databricks and Fabric, Hudi targets upserts.

lessons.title: Object storage: ADLS, S3 and GCS
lessons.summary: Cloud data lakes sit on object storage: virtually unlimited, cheap, durable storage of files (objects) addressed by key.
lessons.remember: Object storage is the cheap, durable, shared foundation of every lakehouse, but it is not a file system: mind small files, listing and egress.

lessons.title: Table format interoperability
lessons.summary: Because platforms favour different formats, several mechanisms let one table be read as another: - Delta UniForm: a Delta table also writes Iceberg metadata, so Iceberg readers can read it.
lessons.remember: UniForm, OneLake virtualization, XTable and Iceberg REST catalogs let one copy be read in several formats, with feature and permission caveats.

lessons.title: Apache Spark in the landscape
lessons.summary: Apache Spark is a general-purpose distributed processing engine: one engine for batch ETL, SQL, streaming and machine learning, with APIs in Python, SQL, Scala, Java and R.
lessons.remember: Spark is the general-purpose distributed engine for big batch, streaming and ML; use smaller engines when data fits on one machine.

lessons.title: Trino and Presto
lessons.summary: Presto was created at Facebook as a fast distributed SQL engine for interactive queries over data lakes.
lessons.remember: Trino (and PrestoDB) are distributed SQL engines for interactive, federated queries over lakes and databases; Athena is serverless Trino.

lessons.title: dbt
lessons.summary: dbt ("data build tool") is the standard way to manage SQL transformations inside a warehouse or lakehouse.
lessons.remember: dbt manages SQL transformations as tested, documented, dependency-ordered models that the warehouse runs.

lessons.title: DuckDB
lessons.summary: DuckDB is an in-process analytical database: a library you import into Python, R, Java or a command line, like SQLite but built for analytics.
lessons.remember: DuckDB is a fast in-process SQL engine for analytics on one machine, often replacing a cluster for medium-sized data.

lessons.title: Cloud warehouse engines
lessons.summary: A cloud data warehouse is a managed SQL engine for analytics: columnar storage, massively parallel query execution, SQL security and high concurrency, with little or no infrastructure to manage.
lessons.remember: Cloud warehouses are managed, parallel SQL engines; choose by ecosystem, pricing model and openness of storage.

lessons.title: Scheduling vs orchestration
lessons.summary: A scheduler runs a job at a time: cron, Windows Task Scheduler, a SQL Agent job.
lessons.remember: A scheduler starts a job at a time; an orchestrator runs dependent tasks with retries, alerts, parameters and backfills.

lessons.title: Apache Airflow
lessons.summary: Apache Airflow is the most widely used open-source orchestrator.
lessons.remember: Airflow orchestrates Python-defined DAGs of tasks across any system; Airflow 3 added versioning, assets and task isolation.

lessons.title: Dagster
lessons.summary: Dagster is an open-source orchestrator built around software-defined assets: instead of describing tasks, you declare the data assets (tables, files, ML models) your code produces and what they depend on.
lessons.remember: Dagster orchestrates by declaring data assets and their dependencies, giving built-in lineage, freshness and checks.

lessons.title: Prefect
lessons.summary: Prefect is a Python-native workflow orchestrator.
lessons.remember: Prefect turns plain Python functions into orchestrated flows, with a hosted control plane and execution in your own infrastructure.

lessons.title: ADF, Fabric pipelines and Databricks Jobs as orchestrators
lessons.summary: Data platforms ship their own orchestrators: - Azure Data Factory and Fabric Data Factory pipelines: visual pipelines with activities, control flow, schedules and event triggers.
lessons.remember: Use the platform's own orchestrator when work lives on one platform; add a separate orchestrator when workflows span many systems.

lessons.title: Technical, business and enterprise data catalogs
lessons.summary: "Catalog" means three different things, and confusing them causes bad tool decisions: 1.
lessons.remember: Technical catalogs let engines find and secure tables, discovery catalogs help people find data, and governance suites manage policy across platforms.

lessons.title: Unity Catalog in the landscape
lessons.summary: Unity Catalog exists in two forms: - Databricks Unity Catalog: the governance layer of the Databricks platform.
lessons.remember: Databricks Unity Catalog is a full governance layer on Databricks; the open-source Unity Catalog is a smaller, engine-neutral catalog server.

lessons.title: Microsoft Purview
lessons.summary: Microsoft Purview is Microsoft's family of data governance, security and compliance products.
lessons.remember: Purview maps and classifies data across the estate, adds business governance with data products and quality, and supplies the labels, DLP and audit that Fabric uses.

lessons.title: DataHub and OpenMetadata
lessons.summary: Two leading open-source metadata platforms for discovery, lineage and governance across many tools: - DataHub (created at LinkedIn, now under LF AI & Data; 1.x releases): an event-driven architecture where metadata chang
lessons.remember: DataHub and OpenMetadata are open-source, cross-platform catalogs; DataHub is event-driven and extensible, OpenMetadata simpler with built-in quality features.

lessons.title: Data lineage and OpenLineage
lessons.summary: Lineage records how data flows: which jobs read which datasets and wrote which others, and ideally which columns came from which.
lessons.remember: Lineage comes from engines, parsing or OpenLineage events; combine them to see flows across platforms.

lessons.title: Enterprise catalogs: Collibra, Alation, Informatica
lessons.summary: Commercial governance and catalog platforms aimed at large, multi-platform organisations: - Collibra: governance-led, with strong stewardship workflows, business glossary, policy management and data quality; in 2025 it a
lessons.remember: Collibra, Alation and Informatica are cross-platform governance suites for formal governance programmes; their value depends on the people and processes behind them.

lessons.title: Great Expectations
lessons.summary: Great Expectations (the open-source library is now called GX Core, version 1.x since August 2024) is a Python framework for testing data.
lessons.remember: GX Core lets Python pipelines declare expectations about data, validate batches and publish readable results.

lessons.title: Soda
lessons.summary: Soda is a data quality tool where checks are written in YAML rather than code.
lessons.remember: Soda checks data with YAML definitions, and since v4 centres on data contracts verified against each dataset.

lessons.title: Deequ and PyDeequ
lessons.summary: Deequ is an open-source library from AWS Labs, written in Scala on Apache Spark, for "unit tests for data".
lessons.remember: Deequ computes and checks data quality metrics efficiently on Spark, but PyDeequ's JVM dependency limits it on modern Spark Connect platforms.

lessons.title: Data observability platforms
lessons.summary: Data observability applies monitoring ideas from software to data: instead of writing every rule by hand, a platform watches datasets continuously and alerts on anomalies.
lessons.remember: Data observability watches freshness, volume, schema, distribution and lineage automatically to catch the problems no test anticipated.

lessons.title: Data contracts
lessons.summary: A data contract is an explicit, versioned agreement between a data producer (an application team, a source system owner) and its consumers about a dataset: schema (columns, types, meaning), quality rules, freshness and a
lessons.remember: A data contract is an enforced, versioned agreement on schema, quality and ownership between producer and consumers.

lessons.title: ClickHouse
lessons.summary: ClickHouse is an open-source (Apache 2.0) column-oriented OLAP database built for very fast aggregations over large volumes of event-style data.
lessons.remember: ClickHouse is a columnar OLAP database whose sorted MergeTree tables make aggregations over billions of events fast.

lessons.title: Apache Druid and Apache Pinot
lessons.summary: Two open-source real-time OLAP stores built for low-latency queries on fresh event data, often directly from Kafka: - Apache Druid: ingests streams (Kafka, Kinesis) and batches into time-partitioned segments with indexes
lessons.remember: Druid and Pinot serve fresh event data to many concurrent users with millisecond latency; Pinot leans to user-facing analytics.

lessons.title: Power BI
lessons.summary: Power BI is Microsoft's business intelligence tool: - Power BI Desktop (free, Windows) to model data and build reports.
lessons.remember: Power BI pairs a strong semantic model engine with Microsoft's ecosystem, and inside Fabric reads OneLake directly.

lessons.title: Tableau
lessons.summary: Tableau is a visual analytics platform, part of Salesforce since 2019.
lessons.remember: Tableau is Salesforce's visual analytics platform, strongest at exploration, with Tableau Next adding semantics and AI agents.

lessons.title: Semantic layers and metrics stores
lessons.summary: A semantic layer defines business concepts (metrics such as revenue or active customers, dimensions, joins, filters) once, in one place, and exposes them to every consumer: BI tools, notebooks, applications and, increasi
lessons.remember: A semantic layer defines metrics once for every tool and for AI; it lives in the BI tool, the platform, or a universal layer.

lessons.title: Docker and containers
lessons.summary: A container packages an application with its dependencies (Python version, libraries, system packages, configuration) so it runs the same everywhere.
lessons.remember: A container image packages code with its dependencies so the tested artefact is exactly what runs.

lessons.title: Kubernetes
lessons.summary: Kubernetes orchestrates containers across a cluster of machines.
lessons.remember: Kubernetes runs and scales containers declaratively across a cluster; powerful for data services, but it needs a team to operate.

lessons.title: Terraform and infrastructure as code
lessons.summary: Infrastructure as code (IaC) describes cloud resources (storage accounts, networks, Databricks workspaces, Fabric capacities, Snowflake warehouses, permissions) in files kept in Git, and tools create or update the real r
lessons.remember: Terraform declares infrastructure in code, plans changes against stored state and applies them; keep state safe and avoid manual drift.

lessons.title: CI/CD for data platforms
lessons.summary: CI/CD automates checking and deploying changes.
lessons.remember: CI tests every change and CD promotes the same artefact through environments with approvals, using each platform's deployment tooling.

lessons.title: Secrets and identity
lessons.summary: Pipelines need to authenticate to databases, storage and APIs.
lessons.remember: Prefer managed identities and federation over stored secrets; keep unavoidable secrets in a vault and grant least privilege.

lessons.title: MLflow
lessons.summary: MLflow is the most widely used open-source platform for the ML lifecycle (Linux Foundation; version 3.x since mid-2025).
lessons.remember: MLflow records runs, packages models with signatures, registers versions with aliases, and now traces and evaluates GenAI apps.

lessons.title: Feature store products
lessons.summary: A feature store keeps ML features (customer's orders in the last 30 days, average basket size) in two forms: an offline store (warehouse or lake tables for training, with point-in-time correct joins) and an online store
lessons.remember: Feature store products manage offline features for training and online features for serving from one definition; adopt one when features are shared and served in real time.

lessons.title: Vector databases and vector search
lessons.summary: Vector search finds items whose embeddings are closest to a query embedding, the core of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search and recommendations.
lessons.remember: Vector search uses ANN indexes such as HNSW, IVF or DiskANN; start with vector features in your existing platform and add hybrid keyword search.

lessons.title: Model serving platforms
lessons.summary: Model serving puts a trained model behind an API so applications can get predictions in real time.
lessons.remember: Serve models in real time only when needed, using a managed endpoint or a Kubernetes serving framework, with vLLM-style engines for LLMs.

lessons.title: Cloud map: ingestion, streaming and storage
lessons.summary: Each cloud offers a similar set of building blocks under different names.
lessons.remember: Every cloud has object storage, a streaming service, a CDC service and a batch mover; the names differ more than the ideas.

lessons.title: Cloud map: processing and orchestration
lessons.summary: For the processing and orchestration layers: Role AWS Azure Google Cloud ------------ Managed Spark Amazon EMR (EC2, EKS, Serverless), AWS Glue Azure Databricks, Fabric Spark, Synapse Spark (earlier service) Dataproc, Se
lessons.remember: Each cloud pairs managed Spark, serverless SQL, a warehouse, stream processing and an orchestrator; Databricks and Snowflake sit across all three.

lessons.title: Cloud map: governance, BI and ML
lessons.summary: For governance, consumption and ML (names as of October 2026): Role AWS Azure / Microsoft Google Cloud ------------ Technical catalog AWS Glue Data Catalog OneLake catalog, Unity Catalog (Azure Databricks) Dataplex Unive
lessons.remember: Each cloud has a catalog, an access layer, a BI tool and an ML platform; their names change fast, so check current names before designing.
